Title: A Survey of Code-switching: Linguistic and Social Perspectives for Language Technologies
Authors: A. Seza Doğruöz; Sunayana Sitaram; Barbara E. Bullock; Almeida Jacqueline Toribio
Venue: Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (ACL-IJCNLP 2021)
Domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Computational Linguistics, Sociolinguistics, Multilingualism, Code-Switching (C-S) in European and Indian multilingual contact contexts
Problem Statement: Computational linguistics and natural language processing research on code-switching predominantly focuses on algorithmic and computational improvements while ignoring rich linguistic, structural, cognitive, and sociolinguistic theories from linguistics literature, resulting in massive multilingual models that fail to capture diverse code-switching types, lack adequate training data and benchmarks, and omit sociolinguistic dynamics in user-facing applications.
Theoretical Framework: Theoretical linguistic and sociolinguistic frameworks of code-switching, including the Matrix Language Frame (MLF) model (Myers-Scotton; Joshi), Equivalence Constraint (Poplack), Government Constraint (DiSciullo et al.), Functional Head Constraint (Belazi et al.), Constraint-free models (Mahootian & Santorini; MacSwan), Auer's continuum of bilingual speech (prototypical code-switching, language mixing, mixed languages), Politeness theory and face-saving (Lavric), Clyne's eight-factor interactional model, and socio-indexical identity marking/backflagging (Muysken; Poplack; Gumperz; Zentella; Finnis).
Methodology: Cross-disciplinary systematic survey and critical synthesis analyzing structural, functional, cognitive, and sociolinguistic dimensions of code-switching across European and Indian multilingual contexts; contrasting linguistic frameworks against current computational NLP practices; distinguishing code-switching from borrowing, transfer, and loan translation; and evaluating computational bottlenecks across pretraining data in massive multilingual language models (e.g., mBERT, XLM-R), multi-task benchmark evaluation suites (GLUE-CoS, LINCE), and user-facing interactive systems.
Key Findings: Computational linguistics research predominantly relies on the Matrix Language Frame (MLF) model despite empirical and theoretical criticisms regarding matrix language identification and clause-level boundary limits, while under-utilizing alternative grammatical constraints (such as the Functional Head Constraint) that improve computational and speech models.; NLP tag sets and models frequently fail to distinguish between true grammatical code-switching and nonce borrowings, lexical transfer, or loan translations, employing coarse part-of-speech annotations that obscure intra-sentential functional constraints.; Code-switching is strongly driven by pragmatic, cognitive, and socio-indexical functions (such as expressing in-group solidarity, politeness, conversational topic, and affective stance), which leave predictable structural traces that are ignored in conventional NLP pipelines.; Massive pretrained multilingual language models (e.g., mBERT, XLM-R) perform substantially worse on code-switched tasks than monolingual settings because they are trained on web-scraped monolingual corpora (Wikipedia, Common Crawl) lacking natural spoken and informal code-switching varieties.; Standardized code-switching benchmarks (e.g., GLUE-CoS, LINCE) are limited to a narrow set of language pairs (primarily Spanish-English and Hindi-English) and social media domains (Twitter), with state-of-the-art models performing near chance levels on complex reasoning tasks like Natural Language Inference (NLI).; Current language technologies almost entirely lack end-to-end user-facing applications (such as conversational dialogue systems) capable of dynamically adapting to user code-switching styles, social preferences, and affective language choices.; Both linguistics and computational research suffer from a positive-evidence bias by assuming code-switching occurs uniformly across all multilingual communities, ignoring negative evidence where historical, social, and prestige dynamics suppress switching (e.g., Saraswat Brahmin Konkani-Kannada bilinguals).
Scope and Delimitations: Focuses primarily on linguistic, sociolinguistic, and computational perspectives of code-switching within European multilingual contexts (e.g., Turkish-German, Frisian-Dutch, Spanish-Catalan, Russian-Ukrainian) and Indian multilingual contexts (Indo-Aryan and Dravidian language contact, Hindi-English, Bengali-English).; Delimits computational analysis to three primary bottlenecks: pretraining data representation in massive multilingual language models, multi-task benchmark evaluation suites, and user-facing interactive applications.; Excludes developing new algorithmic architectures or releasing novel empirical datasets, serving instead as a taxonomic and cross-disciplinary bridge between linguistics and computational NLP.
Limitations (Summary): Current computational processing of code-switching is fundamentally limited by three interrelated constraints: the absence of diverse code-switching training data in multilingual language models, narrow evaluation benchmarks covering only simpler NLP tasks over a few language pairs, and a lack of end-to-end user-facing applications that model the sociolinguistic, functional, and pragmatic factors governing human code-switching.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Due to the paucity of user-facing systems and standard benchmarks covering only a handful of simpler NLP tasks, it is likely that we overestimate how well computational models are able to handle C-S. In sum, language technologies for C-S seem to be constrained by the lack of availability of diverse C-S training data, evaluation benchmarks and the absence of user-facing applications. They need to go beyond pattern recognition and grammatical constraints of C-S in order to process and produce C-S the way humans do. Hence, it is important for the CL community to be aware of the vast literature around C-S in linguistics, particularly as we proceed to solving more challenging tasks.
Generalizability Gap: Current computational code-switching research is disproportionately concentrated on a few high-resource pairs (primarily Spanish-English and Hindi-English) and social media text (Twitter), leaving regional dialects, unlisted/minority languages with fewer than 10,000 speakers, spoken conversational interactions, and diverse diaspora/immigrant communities severely underrepresented.
Methodological Gap: Existing multilingual language models rely on web-scale monolingual pretraining corpora and coarse POS annotation schemes that cannot capture fine-grained functional heads or distinguish code-switching from borrowing and transfer; synthetic code-switched generation methods rely on rigid grammatical frameworks (e.g., MLF) that fail to generate natural utterances; and existing research lacks systematic collection and modeling of negative evidence where social context inhibits switching.
Future Work: Incorporating formal linguistic theories (such as the Functional Head Constraint and fine-grained functional tag sets) into multilingual language model pretraining and synthetic code-switching generation.; Developing comprehensive, multi-domain evaluation benchmarks spanning diverse language families, regional dialects, and under-resourced or officially unlisted minority languages.; Designing adaptive end-to-end user-facing dialogue systems that model sociolinguistic factors, user style accommodation, and affective language preferences.; Investigating negative evidence in multilingual communities to systematically identify socio-cultural and contextual factors that inhibit code-switching.; Conducting systematic comparative investigations of code-switching patterns within identical language pairs across domestic and diaspora/immigrant environments (e.g., Hindi-English in India vs. the UK/US).; Establishing interdisciplinary publication and citation guidelines to facilitate knowledge transfer between humanities/linguistics and computational linguistics.

Title: A Survey on Multi-Task Learning
Authors: Yu Zhang; Qiang Yang
Venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
Domain: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence (including Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing, Speech Processing, Bioinformatics, Health Informatics, and Web Applications)
Problem Statement: How to systematically categorize, formulate, optimize, and theoretically analyze multi-task learning algorithms across diverse learning paradigms, high-dimensional settings, and application domains to improve task generalization performance.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-task learning foundational frameworks including task relatedness formulations (when to share, what to share, and how to share via feature, instance, or parameter sharing), statistical learning theory (generalization error bounds, Rademacher complexity, local Rademacher complexity, VC dimension, covering numbers, algorithmic stability), matrix and tensor trace norm regularization, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling (matrix-variate normal distributions, Dirichlet processes, and Gaussian processes).
Methodology: Taxonomic survey and analytical synthesis categorizing multi-task learning models into five foundational algorithmic approaches (feature learning, low-rank, task clustering, task relation learning, and parameter decomposition) alongside regularized formulations (feature covariance versus task relation learning), integration with other learning paradigms (semi-supervised, active, unsupervised, reinforcement, multi-view learning, and graphical models), big data scaling techniques (parallel, online, distributed, and federated), and empirical benchmark comparisons.
Key Findings: Multi-task learning algorithms primarily operate along five foundational paradigms: feature learning (feature transformation and feature selection), low-rank approaches, task clustering, task relation learning, and parameter decomposition.; Most regularized multi-task learning methods can be unified under a dual taxonomy: learning with feature covariance (modeling column relations) versus learning with task covariance (modeling task relationships).; In empirical comparisons across benchmark datasets, multi-task learning models consistently outperform single-task learning counterparts by effectively leveraging shared cross-task structures.; Deep multi-task learning models dominate computer vision and natural language processing applications through shared feature representations, whereas bioinformatics and health informatics prioritize interpretable models based on feature selection and task relation learning.; In theoretical analyses of multi-task generalization bounds, methods based on local Rademacher complexity derive tighter generalization bounds than those based on standard VC dimension, covering numbers, and algorithmic stability.
Scope and Delimitations: The survey focuses primarily on multi-task learning where all tasks are treated equally with bidirectional knowledge sharing, explicitly excluding transfer learning (where a single target task is privileged), continual/lifelong learning (where tasks arrive sequentially), and multi-label learning/multi-output regression (where different outputs always share the exact same training instances).; The algorithmic review focuses primarily on supervised multi-task learning (homogeneous-feature and homogeneous-task settings by default), with secondary coverage of extensions to non-supervised paradigms, heterogeneous features, and big data scaling.; The survey focuses predominantly on feature-based and parameter-based multi-task learning methods, reviewing only representative works for instance-based multi-task learning due to the limited number of studies in that area.
Limitations (Summary): Multi-task learning models remain vulnerable to negative transfer caused by unrelated or outlier tasks, lack comprehensive theoretical analyses and principled mechanisms to mitigate negative interference, rely on rigid shared-layer deep architectures susceptible to noisy tasks, and remain predominantly concentrated on supervised learning settings with limited exploration into unsupervised, semi-supervised, active, reinforcement, and multi-view learning.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Firstly, outlier tasks, which are unrelated to other tasks, are well known to hamper the performance of all the tasks when learning them jointly. There are some methods to alleviate negative effects that outlier tasks bring. However, there lacks principled ways and theoretical analyses to study the resulting negative effects. In order to make MTL safe to be used by human, this is an important issue and needs more studies. Secondly, deep learning has become a dominant approach in many areas and several multi-task deep models belonging to the feature transformation, low-rank, task clustering and task relation learning approaches have been proposed as reviewed in Sections 2, 3 and 5. As discussed, most of them only share hidden layers. This approach is powerful when all the tasks are related, but it is vulnerable to noisy and outlier tasks that can deteriorate the performance dramatically. We believe that it is desirable to design flexible and robust deep multi-task models. Lastly, existing studies mainly focus on supervised learning tasks, and only a few ones are on other tasks such as unsupervised learning, semi-supervised learning, active learning, multi-view learning and reinforcement learning tasks.
Generalizability Gap: Most existing multi-task learning literature is concentrated in standard supervised benchmark datasets and single-layer sharing paradigms, leaving open questions regarding scalability and robustness in non-supervised learning paradigms (unsupervised, semi-supervised, active, and reinforcement learning), non-standard task modalities (heterogeneous feature spaces and multi-modal tensors), and complex real-world environments containing high ratios of unrelated or adversarial outlier tasks.
Methodological Gap: Current multi-task learning methodologies lack principled theoretical frameworks and adaptive algorithmic mechanisms to handle outlier tasks and prevent negative transfer; deep multi-task architectures largely rely on rudimentary parameter-sharing structures without automated decision mechanisms for 'when to share'; and direct extensions from binary to multi-class classification remain theoretically and empirically underexplored for task clustering and relation learning approaches.
Future Work: Developing principled methodologies and theoretical analyses to detect outlier tasks and mitigate negative transfer effects.; Designing flexible, adaptive, and robust deep multi-task architectures beyond simple hidden-layer sharing to handle noisy task relationships.; Extending multi-task learning formulations and the five core algorithmic approaches to non-supervised settings, including unsupervised, semi-supervised, active, reinforcement, and multi-view learning.; Applying multi-task learning to broader artificial intelligence domains such as automated reasoning, logic, and planning.; Investigating automated mechanisms for the 'when to share' decision problem to determine whether single-task or multi-task learning is optimal.

Title: BATAYAN: A Filipino NLP benchmark for evaluating Large Language Models
Authors: Jann Railey Montalan; Jimson Paulo Layacan; David Demitri Africa; Richell Isaiah Flores; Michael T. Lopez II; Theresa Denise Magsajo; Anjanette Cayabyab; William Chandra Tjhi
Venue: Preprint (SEA-HELM)
Domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Filipino and Tagalog-English Code-Switching (Taglish), Large Language Model Evaluation, Low-Resource Languages
Problem Statement: Large language models demonstrate high performance on major high-resource languages, but under-resourced languages such as Filipino remain under-represented and linguistically unexamined. Prior Filipino NLP evaluation resources suffered from fragmentation, limited task diversity, domain specificity, translationese bias from unverified automated translations, and poor handling of agglutinative morphology, syntactic word order variations (karaniwang ayos versus di-karaniwang ayos), and Taglish code-switching.
Theoretical Framework: Official Filipino linguistic and translation standards from the Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino (Almario, 2014, 2016); Filipino syntactic theory contrasting predicate-initial natural order (karaniwang ayos) with topicalized inverted order (di-karaniwang ayos / ay-inversion) and discourse continuity frameworks (Tanawan et al., 2008; Malicsi, 2013; Kroeger, 1993; Fox, 1985; Bolata, 2022); translationese theory (Gellerstam, 1986; Riley et al., 2020); and holistic multilingual language model benchmarking frameworks (HELM by Liang et al., 2023; BHASA by Leong et al., 2023; XTREME by Hu et al., 2020).
Methodology: The authors developed BATAYAN, an eight-task benchmark evaluating LLMs across Natural Language Understanding (NLU: Paraphrase Identification, Question Answering, Sentiment Analysis, Toxicity Detection), Natural Language Reasoning (NLR: Causal Reasoning, Natural Language Inference), and Natural Language Generation (NLG: Abstractive Summarization, Machine Translation English-to-Filipino and Filipino-to-English). The curation workflow generated 3,800 test instances and five-shot exemplars through native translation using Helsinki-NLP OPUS-MT followed by human revision (PAWS, Balanced COPA, XNLI, XL-Sum), native re-translation of translated corpora (Belebele QA, FLORES-200 MT) to eliminate translationese bias and favor natural predicate-initial sentence order, and repurposing natively-sourced Philippine election tweets for sentiment analysis and toxicity detection. Dataset quality control applied three-rater native speaker consensus over binary criteria (completeness, fluency, sensibility) and multi-dimensional scaled criteria (faithfulness, relevance, coherence for summarization). The authors evaluated over 50 LLMs across small (<=11B), medium (<=32B), large (>=32B), and commercial model categories under zero-shot prompting for instruction-tuned models and five-shot prompting for base pre-trained models.
Datasets and Benchmarks: BATAYAN: An overarching benchmark containing 3,800 test instances across 8 tasks spanning NLU, NLR, and NLG competencies in Filipino and Taglish; PAWS (Paraphrase Adversaries from Word Scrambling): 400 test samples natively translated from English for Filipino Paraphrase Identification (PI); Belebele: 100 test samples natively re-translated from machine-translated Filipino for Reading Comprehension Question Answering (QA); Philippine Election Tweets (Cabasag et al., 2019): 600 test samples natively annotated for 3-class Sentiment Analysis (SA) and 400 test samples for Toxicity Detection (TD); Balanced COPA (Choice of Plausible Alternatives): 400 test samples natively translated from English for Causal Reasoning (CR); XNLI (Cross-lingual Natural Language Inference): 600 test samples natively translated from English for Natural Language Inference (NLI); XL-Sum: 100 test samples natively translated and manually summarized for Abstractive Summarization (AS); FLORES-200: 1,200 test samples (600 English->Filipino, 600 Filipino->English) natively re-translated for Machine Translation (MT)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Macro F1 (NLU and NLR tasks: PI, QA, SA, TD, CR, NLI); ChrF++ (Machine Translation and Abstractive Summarization); MetricX-24 using metricx-24-hybrid-xxl-v2p6-bfloat16 (Machine Translation); BERTScore (Abstractive Summarization); ROUGE-L F1 (Multilingual ROUGE implementation for Abstractive Summarization); Cohen's Kappa and Krippendorff's Alpha (Inter-annotator agreement for Sentiment Analysis annotation); Joint Agreement (Human acceptability judgment on completeness, fluency, and sensibility)]; evaluated models: (small models under 11b: ['aisingapore/Gemma-SEA-LION-v3-9B (Base and IT)', 'aisingapore/Llama-SEA-LION-v2-8B (Base and IT)', 'aisingapore/Llama-SEA-LION-v3-8B (Base and IT)', 'google/gemma-2-9b (Base and IT)', 'meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B (Base and Instruct)', 'Qwen/Qwen2-7B (Base and Instruct)', 'Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B (Base and Instruct)', 'sail/Sailor2-8B (Base and Chat)', 'SeaLLMs/SeaLLMs-v3-7B (Base and Chat)', 'CohereForAI/aya-23-8B', 'CohereForAI/aya-expanse-8b', 'MERaLiON/Llama-3-MERaLiON-8B-Instruct', 'Tower-Babel/Babel-9B-Chat'], medium models under 32b: ['google/gemma-2-27b (Base and IT)', 'google/gemma-3-12b-pt (Base and IT)', 'google/gemma-3-27b-pt (Base and IT)', 'Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B (Base and Instruct)', 'Qwen/Qwen2.5-32B (Base and Instruct)', 'sail/Sailor2-20B (Base and Chat)', 'CohereForAI/aya-expanse-32b'], large models over 32b: ['aisingapore/Llama-SEA-LION-v3-70B (Base and IT)', 'meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B (Base and Instruct)', 'meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct', 'Qwen/Qwen2-72B (Base and Instruct)', 'Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B (Base and Instruct)', 'CohereForAI/aya-23-35B', 'deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3', 'deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1', 'Tower-Babel/Babel-83B-Chat'], commercial models: ['google/gemini-1.5-flash-002', 'google/gemini-1.5-pro-002', 'google/gemini-2.0-flash-001', 'google/gemini-2.0-flash-lite-001', 'openai/gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18', 'openai/gpt-4o-2024-08-06']); inter annotator agreement: (sentiment analysis annotation: Cohen's kappa = 0.8202, Krippendorff's alpha = 0.8268 (substantial agreement), quality filtering: 3/3 rater unanimous joint agreement on binary criteria (completeness, fluency, sensibility))
Key Findings: The authors created BATAYAN, a native-speaker-validated benchmark of 3,800 test instances across 8 tasks, introducing the first Filipino evaluation datasets for abstractive summarization, causal reasoning, and paraphrase identification.; Dedicated Filipino instruction tuning produces large performance gains on culturally and morphologically nuanced tasks; Gemma-SEA-LION-v3-9B-IT attained an average macro F1 of 79.23 on small-model NLU and 92.75 on causal reasoning, whereas non-adapted models such as Llama-3 variants scored near zero on causal reasoning.; Automated translations of English corpora exhibited systemic translationese bias, including an unnatural preference for inverted word order (di-karaniwang ayos / ay-inversion) and pragmatically awkward word choices, which native human re-translation corrected into natural predicate-initial constructions (karaniwang ayos).; Model performance exhibited clear scaling effects across parameter sizes (7B to 671B), demonstrating that greater model capacity combined with regional instruction tuning significantly improves the representation of agglutinative morphology, focus marking, and Taglish code-switching.; Open-source models with dedicated Filipino tuning (such as Gemma-SEA-LION-v3-9B-IT and Llama-SEA-LION-v3-70B-IT) achieved performance competitive with or superior to top commercial models (Gemini 1.5/2.0 and GPT-4o variants) on Filipino natural language understanding and reasoning tasks.; Semantic evaluation metrics such as MetricX-24 revealed significant translation quality advantages (MetricX-24 >87 for Filipino-tuned models) that surface-level lexical overlap metrics such as ROUGE-L failed to detect.
Scope and Delimitations: The benchmark focuses exclusively on Filipino (Tagalog) and Tagalog-English code-switched (Taglish) text, excluding other regional Philippine languages.; Task scope is delimited to eight specific NLP tasks: Paraphrase Identification, Question Answering, Sentiment Analysis, Toxicity Detection, Causal Reasoning, Natural Language Inference, Abstractive Summarization, and Machine Translation.; Benchmark volume is delimited to 3,800 high-quality test instances (100 to 1,200 samples per task) selected through strict unanimous three-rater acceptability criteria rather than large unverified web scrapes.; Social media data for sentiment analysis and toxicity detection is delimited to Philippine election-related tweets from 2019.; Model evaluation is delimited to zero-shot inference for instruction-tuned models and five-shot in-context learning for base pre-trained models.
Limitations (Summary): The authors identify several study limitations: prosodic features such as stress and sarcasm are difficult to identify in text datasets; sentiment analysis and toxicity detection corpora are restricted to political election tweets; total dataset size is delimited to 3,800 instances because the authors prioritized manual native quality filtering over dataset volume; and broad benchmark scope prevented comprehensive qualitative error analysis or evaluation on specialized translation models.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt):
While our work provides a unique and comprehensive Filipino language benchmark, we also reported in previous sections the challenges and limitations in developing high-quality NLP resources for the under-represented language. Additionally, prosodic characteristics such as stress and sarcasm are not immediately obvious in the datasets utilized. We account for this by selecting only high-agreement samples. We also note that the domain of both SA and TD tasks (which were tweets surrounding political events), limits the distributions of these tasks, and as such we recommend utilizing other datasets that cover a wider set of domains and use cases.

While we recognize that datasets with larger amounts of samples are preferred to ensure generalizability, we maintain our position to prioritize consistent, high-quality, and representative samples.
Generalizability Gap: The benchmark evaluates only Filipino/Tagalog and Taglish text within written formats, leaving unexamined the more than 100 other Philippine regional languages (such as Cebuano, Ilocano, and Hiligaynon), spoken modalities, and non-political domain distributions for sentiment and toxicity tasks.
Methodological Gap: Automated lexical evaluation metrics such as ROUGE-L lack sensitivity to semantic fidelity and morphological subtleties in agglutinative Filipino text; tools to automatically differentiate translationese from natural text remain unavailable; subjective stylistic preferences for sentence order (karaniwang ayos versus di-karaniwang ayos) introduce minor syntactic variance; and the study did not include comprehensive qualitative error category breakdowns.
Future Work: Developing automated metrics and classification tools to discriminate translationese from natural Filipino text.; Expanding the benchmark to larger sample sizes, diverse non-political domains, and broader social media use cases.; Conducting detailed error analyses to characterize model failure modes across specific morphological and syntactic structures.; Evaluating specialized language models and extending benchmarking frameworks to other regional languages of the Philippines.; Maintaining and expanding the public evaluation suite and leaderboard on SEA-HELM for collaborative progress in Southeast Asian NLP.

Title: Beyond Monolingual Assumptions: A Survey on Code-Switched NLP in the Era of Large Language Models across Modalities
Authors: Rajvee Sheth; Samridhi Raj Sinha; Mahavir Patil; Himanshu Beniwal; Mayank Singh
Domain: Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, Code-Switching and Code-Mixing, Multilingual Computing, Multimodal AI (Speech and Vision-Language Processing), Low-Resource Languages
Problem Statement: How Large Language Models handle code-switched inputs across text, speech, and vision-language modalities, why multilingual pre-training fails to guarantee robust code-switching performance, and how existing architectural designs, dataset shortages, and evaluation biases restrict effective deployment in multilingual societies.
Theoretical Framework: Sociolinguistic and grammatical theories of code-switching (including Poplack's Equivalence Constraint model and structural switch-point constraints), quantitative code-mixing metrics (Code-Mixing Index [CMI], S-index, M-index, I-index, and SyM-CoM), cross-lingual representation alignment in foundation models, and multimodal fusion architectures.
Methodology: Systematic literature review and taxonomic synthesis analyzing 327 studies across 15+ NLP tasks, 30+ datasets, and 80+ languages; categorizing research into pre-LLM versus LLM eras, five core research directions, training paradigms (pre-training, fine-tuning, instruction tuning, PEFT, RLAIF), multimodal speech and vision applications, and evaluation methodologies to identify persistent failure modes and outline a future research roadmap.
Key Findings: Multilingual pre-training alone does not ensure code-switching proficiency; large language models frequently underperform compared to smaller, task-specific fine-tuned models on code-switched inputs because pre-training corpora contain limited naturalistic code-switched data.; Large language models exhibit asymmetric transfer and language confusion; models process English tokens embedded within non-English contexts better than non-English tokens within English contexts, and standard fine-tuning amplifies unintended language generation.; Current code-switching research exhibits extreme resource concentration; over 72% of speech datasets and 92% of social media code-switching datasets involve English (predominantly Hindi-English, Spanish-English, and Mandarin-English), leaving non-English pairs, African languages, Southeast Asian languages, and trilingual settings critically underexplored.; Synthetic code-switching generation methods expand training volume but achieve only 60% to 65% human acceptability, failing to capture spontaneous conversational behavior, orthographic variations, transliteration nuances, and sociolinguistic pragmatic intent.; Standard evaluation metrics (such as BLEU, Word Error Rate, and perplexity) and LLM-as-a-judge evaluators correlate poorly with human judgments on code-switched generation and speech tasks, overestimating model performance and failing to capture switch-point dynamics.; Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, curriculum-based instruction tuning, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback improve low-resource adaptation, but speech and vision-language multimodal code-switching systems lag significantly behind text-based natural language understanding.
Scope and Delimitations: The survey synthesizes academic research on code-switched natural language processing, focusing primarily on large language models and foundation models while contextualizing historical methods from statistical and neural eras.; The review spans 15+ natural language processing tasks across token-level, sentence-level, generation, conversational, reasoning, speech, and vision-language modalities across 80+ languages.; The analysis examines academic literature and public benchmark datasets, delimiting coverage of proprietary industrial deployment constraints and production infrastructure optimizations.; The survey reports representative quantitative metrics from cited primary studies rather than conducting independent experimental evaluations or statistical meta-analyses.
Limitations (Summary): The survey exhibits coverage bias toward widely studied language pairs while potentially omitting indigenous or minority languages, faces rapid obsolescence due to fast-evolving foundation model paradigms, covers text-based understanding more comprehensively than speech and multimodal processing due to literature availability, focuses primarily on academic progress rather than real-world industrial deployment considerations, and compiles representative findings from primary literature rather than computing aggregated statistical meta-analyses.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt):
Despite providing a broad survey, this paper has several limitations:

- 1. Coverage Bias The survey highlights widely studied language pairs and might have missed indigenous or minority code-mixed languages.
- 2. Evolving Landscape Given the rapid pace of LLM research, some approaches and benchmarks described may soon be outdated or replaced by newer paradigms.
- 3. Evaluation Constraints While we include recent advances in speech and multimodal processing, the volume of research in these areas significantly lags behind text-based NLU, resulting in our taxonomy covering more text based NLU.
- 4. Practical deployment The survey mainly covers academic progress, leaving ethical, computational, and accessibility concerns in real-world deployment less examined.
- 5. Quantitative Reporting All quantitative claims are representative values reported in the cited primary works rather than aggregated or meta-analyzed statistics.
Generalizability Gap: Large Language Models and code-switching benchmarks demonstrate limited cross-linguistic and cross-regional generalizability, showing 25% to 35% performance drops when tested across different geographic varieties of the same language pair. Furthermore, empirical resources remain heavily concentrated in English-centric bilingual pairs (over 72% of speech and 92% of social media datasets), leaving low-resource African, Dravidian, and Southeast Asian language pairs, non-Latin script transliterations, and trilingual switching settings critically underexplored.
Methodological Gap: Current code-switching methodologies suffer from three fundamental shortcomings: (1) pre-training relies predominantly on monolingual corpora and synthetic code-switched data that achieves only 60% to 65% human acceptability, failing to model natural conversational switch points; (2) standard evaluation metrics (BLEU, Word Error Rate, perplexity) and LLM-as-a-judge frameworks fail to capture discourse coherence, sociolinguistic intent, and dialectal nuances; and (3) architectural designs lack specialized script-aware and switch-point-aware mechanisms, leading to language confusion and jailbreak safety vulnerabilities under mixed-language prompts.
Future Work: Developing inclusive, naturalistic conversational datasets for underrepresented and low-resource language pairs with participatory community curation and human-in-the-loop validation.; Designing next-generation multimodal architectures that jointly model text, speech, and vision with switch-point detection, phonemic grounding, and mixture-of-experts routing.; Establishing holistic, human-aligned evaluation paradigms that assess switch-point accuracy, semantic consistency, discourse coherence, and sociolinguistic appropriateness beyond rigid lexical matching.; Investigating multilingual safety alignment and ethical frameworks to mitigate jailbreaks, backdoor attacks, and cultural biases in code-switched systems.; Expanding code-switching research to trilingual discourse, non-Latin script transliteration normalization, and complex cross-lingual reasoning tasks.

Title: Classification of Local Language Disaster Related Tweets in Micro Blogs
Authors: Randy Joy Magno Ventayen
Venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Multidisciplinary Research
Domain: Disaster Response and Crisis Informatics, Natural Language Processing for low-resource regional Philippine languages (Pangasinan microblog tweets during typhoons in Region 1, Philippines)
Problem Statement: Social media disaster monitoring tools predominantly focus on major languages such as English and Tagalog, leaving non-English and regional dialect speakers (specifically Pangasinan speakers in Region 1, Philippines) underserved during disaster response and emergency relief operations.
Theoretical Framework: Social media-based situational awareness and crisis informatics for disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) in low-resource local languages
Methodology: The author developed a pipeline comprising: (1) Python-based Twitter data acquisition via the Twitter REST API and Tweepy using disaster hashtags (#LawinPH and #KarenPH); (2) manual keyword translation using interviews with native elderly Pangasinan speakers and a mobile Pangasinan-English Dictionary app to construct a disaster lexicon; (3) keyword-based filtering of downloaded tweets; (4) a simulated data collection experiment involving 46 student participants to generate 217 Pangasinan tweets due to natural data scarcity; and (5) word-frequency feature extraction and automated binary classification (disaster-related vs. non-disaster-related) using Support Vector Machines (SVM) in RapidMiner.
Datasets and Benchmarks: Filtered organic Twitter dataset collected with hashtag #LawinPH (October 17-22, 2016), yielding 12 Pangasinan tweets; Synthetic Pangasinan disaster tweet dataset created by 46 student participants generating 217 tweets (100 used for training, 117 for testing)
Evaluation and Metrics: classifier: Support Vector Machine (SVM); training samples: 100; testing samples: 117; accuracy: 89.74% (105/117); true positive rate: 90.00% (54/60); true negative rate: 89.47% (51/57)
Key Findings: Manual translation of disaster keywords using native speaker interviews and dictionary tools enabled effective keyword-based filtering of regional Pangasinan tweets from a broader microblog corpus.; Real-world data extraction during Typhoon Lawin yielded only 12 organic Pangasinan tweets using disaster hashtags, demonstrating extreme data sparsity for local dialects in social media microblogs.; A Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier trained on 100 simulated Pangasinan tweets achieved 89.74% overall accuracy, 90.00% true positive rate, and 89.47% true negative rate on a test set of 117 tweets.; Frequency-based feature extraction paired with machine learning classification can reliably distinguish disaster-related from non-disaster-related content in regional low-resource languages.

Title: Code-Switched Named Entity Recognition with Embedding Attention
Authors: Changhan Wang; Kyunghyun Cho; Douwe Kiela
Venue: Proceedings of the Third Workshop on Computational Approaches to Linguistic Code-Switching (CALCS 2018)
Domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Named Entity Recognition (NER), Linguistic Code-Switching, Social Media (Twitter), Multilingual Representation Learning
Problem Statement: Standard natural language processing pipelines experience severe performance deterioration on code-switched text, creating a need for effective named entity recognition models capable of handling noisy, multilingual social media data across diverse language pairs.
Theoretical Framework: Neural sequence labeling integrating pre-trained multi-source word embeddings, character-level recurrent representations, self-attention mechanisms for dynamic modality fusion, shortcut-stacked recurrent sentence encoding, and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) for structured output prediction.
Methodology: An end-to-end neural sequence tagging architecture comprising four main components: (1) multi-level representations integrating language-specific FastText embeddings trained on Common Crawl and Wikipedia, character-level BiLSTMs with max-pooling, and explicit capitalization embeddings; (2) an embedding-level self-attention mechanism that computes dynamic task-specific weights across multilingual and character-level embeddings without contextual dependencies; (3) multi-layer shortcut-stacked bidirectional LSTM sentence encoders with residual skip connections; and (4) linear-chain Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) comparing unigram and bigram emission/transition potential scoring functions. Preprocessing normalizes noisy Twitter tokens (URLs, user mentions, hashtags, punctuation, numbers, dates, times, emojis) and strips leading/trailing punctuation for Arabic tokens.
Datasets and Benchmarks: CALCS 2018 Shared Task MSA-EGY: Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian Arabic tweets (10,102 train / 1,122 validation / 1,110 test); CALCS 2018 Shared Task ENG-SPA: English-Spanish tweets (50,757 train / 832 validation / 15,634 test); FastText pre-trained crawl and Wikipedia word vectors for Arabic, Egyptian Arabic, English, and Spanish
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Precision; Recall; Entity F1]; results: (MSA EGY: {'overall': {'Precision': 73.95, 'Recall': 69.42, 'Entity_F1': 71.62}, 'per_category_f1': {'EVENT': 68.8, 'GROUP': 73.17, 'LOC': 71.78, 'ORG': 66.67, 'OTHER': 100.0, 'PER': 73.21, 'PROD': 77.61, 'TIME': 67.92, 'TITLE': 41.38}, 'best_configuration': '4-layer shortcut-stacked BiLSTM [64, 64, 128, 128] with unigram CRF', 'competition_rank': '1st place'}, ENG SPA: {'overall': {'Precision': 70.62, 'Recall': 55.88, 'Entity_F1': 62.39}, 'per_category_f1': {'EVENT': 29.51, 'GROUP': 42.86, 'LOC': 69.98, 'ORG': 37.93, 'OTHER': 3.08, 'PER': 72.09, 'PROD': 54.46, 'TIME': 43.24, 'TITLE': 33.83}, 'best_single_configuration': '3-layer shortcut-stacked BiLSTM [128, 128, 128] with bigram CRF', 'ensemble_f1': 62.67, 'competition_rank': '3rd place'})
Key Findings: The embedding attention neural architecture achieved 1st place on the CALCS 2018 Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian task (71.62 Entity F1) and 3rd place on the English-Spanish task (62.39 Entity F1, 62.67 with ensembling), outperforming standard concatenation baselines.; Specialized token preprocessing for social media noise (normalizing numbers, dates, times, emojis, and Arabic punctuation) substantially boosted performance on temporal and event categories (EVENT and TIME).; Explicit capitalization embeddings improved recognition accuracy for PERSON, LOCATION, and ORGANIZATION entities.; Recognition performance varied across entity types: TITLE was consistently challenging across both language pairs (33.83 F1 for ENG-SPA, 41.38 F1 for MSA-EGY), whereas OTHER scored 100.00 F1 on MSA-EGY but only 3.08 F1 on ENG-SPA.; Optimal CRF and hidden layer architectures differed between tasks: a 4-layer stacked BiLSTM with unigram CRF performed best for MSA-EGY, whereas a 3-layer stacked BiLSTM with bigram CRF performed best for ENG-SPA.
Scope and Delimitations: Evaluated on two code-switched language pairs: Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian (closely related varieties) and English-Spanish (distinct languages) using Twitter data.; Deliberately excluded contextual dependencies from the embedding attention mechanism to ensure computational efficiency within competition deadlines.; Kept pre-trained FastText word embeddings frozen during neural training, restricting parameter updates to character BiLSTMs and capitalization embeddings.; Deliberately avoided external gazetteers or complex hand-crafted features to maintain a generalizable neural architecture.
Limitations (Summary): The authors acknowledge several constraints: (1) a severe validation set size imbalance in the English-Spanish dataset (832 development tokens versus 15.6k test tokens) hindered reliable hyperparameter tuning; (2) tight competition deadlines prevented the implementation of contextual dependencies in the attention mechanism and proper ensemble methods; and (3) the model operated without gazetteers, which may have limited performance on difficult low-resource categories such as titles.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): The dev set for this task was very small (832, versus a test set of 15.6k), which explains the discrepancy between dev set and test set performance—this discrepancy also made it difficult to tune hyperparameters properly for this task. We also tried a very simple ensembling strategy, where we took our top three models and randomly sampled a response, which only marginally improved test score performance to 62.67. We did not pursue proper ensembling due to time constraints.
Generalizability Gap: The architecture was evaluated strictly on Twitter social media data across two specific language combinations (MSA-EGY and ENG-SPA). The performance of the model remains unexamined on other language families (such as Indic or Austronesian code-switched pairs), non-Twitter textual genres (such as conversational transcripts, clinical text, or formal news), and higher degrees of intra-word morphological mixing.
Methodological Gap: The embedding attention module operates without contextual dependency across sentence tokens, relying on static pre-trained word vectors rather than contextualized multilingual language representations (such as multilingual BERT or XLM-RoBERTa). Additionally, the system lacks qualitative attention attribution to determine whether the model dynamically attends to language switch points.
Future Work: Analyze the learned attention weights to determine whether the model learns to identify and adapt to code-switching points dynamically via embedding attention.; Incorporate contextual dependencies into the embedding attention mechanism.; Explore sophisticated model ensembling strategies and examine the integration of external lexical gazetteers without compromising the flexibility of the neural architecture.

Title: COMI-LINGUA: Expert Annotated Large-Scale Dataset for Multitask NLP in Hindi-English Code-Mixing
Authors: Rajvee Sheth; Himanshu Beniwal; Mayank Singh
Domain: Multilingual Natural Language Processing (NLP), Code-Mixing / Code-Switching, Hindi-English (Hinglish) across Roman and Devanagari scripts from social media, news portals, and digital archives.
Problem Statement: The lack of large-scale, high-quality, human-annotated datasets and standardized benchmarks for Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-mixing across both Devanagari and Roman scripts and diverse core NLP tasks, which limits the training, evaluation, and diagnostic error analysis of multilingual large language models on complex code-mixed text.
Theoretical Framework: Matrix Language Frame theory (specifically Matrix Language Identification to determine the dominant language dictating syntactic structure) and Code-Mixing Index (CMI) formulation for quantifying code-mixing intensity.
Methodology: The authors curate raw Hinglish text from news portals, social media platforms (X, YouTube), political channels, and official archives, filtering sentences by Code-Mixing Index (CMI >= 9), sentence length (>= 5 tokens), profanity, and hate speech. They employ a two-stage annotation pipeline using the COMMENTATOR framework where initial pre-annotations generated by NLP tools and LLMs (Microsoft LID, CodeSwitch, LLaMA 3.3) are manually reviewed and corrected by three bilingual graduate-level experts across five core tasks (LID, MLI, NER, POS tagging, and Machine Translation into Standard English, Romanized Hindi, and Devanagari Hindi), resolving conflicts via majority voting (>= 2/3 agreement). They benchmark traditional tools (Microsoft LID, codeswitch), open-weight LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Aya-Expanse-8B, Qwen2.5-7B), and closed-weight LLMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Command-A-03-2025) under zero-shot and one-shot in-context learning, and perform LoRA parameter-efficient fine-tuning on 7-8B open-weight models.
Datasets and Benchmarks: COMI-LINGUA (125,615 filtered instances; 376,845 manual expert annotations across LID, MLI, NER, POS tagging, and MT); Supplementary seed data from prior corpora: PHINC (Srivastava & Singh, 2020), MUTANT (Gupta et al., 2023), Singh et al. (2018c), and YouTube video transcripts (Hugging Face); News and web sources: NDTV, ABP News, Zee News, News18, TV9, Aaj Tak, X (Twitter), YouTube, INC/BJP/AAP political channels, Mann Ki Baat, Press Information Bureau (PIB)
Evaluation and Metrics: inter annotator agreement: Fleiss' Kappa >= 0.817 across all classification tasks (LID: 0.834, MLI: 0.976, NER: 0.852, POS: 0.817; average: 0.863); metrics: Macro Precision, Recall, and Macro F1-score for LID, MLI, NER, and POS; BLEU and chrF++ for Machine Translation evaluated disaggregated across Standard English (Ben, cFen), Romanized Hindi (Brh, cFrh), and Devanagari Hindi (Bdh, cFdh); zero shot findings: Closed-weight LLMs dominate zero-shot performance (GPT-4o: LID F1 92.7, MLI F1 98.1, NER F1 60.1, POS F1 70.1; Claude 3.5 Sonnet: LID F1 92.1, MLI F1 90.0, NER F1 56.7, POS F1 69.0), while traditional specialized tools like codeswitch outperform zero-shot LLMs on POS tagging (88.2 F1); one shot findings: One-shot prompting consistently boosts performance across LLMs and tasks, especially for structure-sensitive tasks like NER (Claude 3.5 Sonnet NER F1 increases from 56.7 to 85.0) and MT (LLaMA-3.3-70B achieves 62.2 BLEU in English translation); fine tuning findings: LoRA fine-tuning of 7-8B open-weight LLMs on COMI-LINGUA yields dramatic gains over prompting (LLaMA-3.1-8B achieves 94.75 F1 in LID, 93.05 F1 in MLI, 95.25 F1 in NER, 86.17 F1 in POS, 56.1 BLEU in English MT, 73.5 BLEU in Devanagari MT; Aya-Expanse-8B achieves 98.77 F1 in MLI, 94.90 F1 in NER, 88.61 F1 in POS)
Key Findings: COMI-LINGUA is established as the largest manually annotated Hinglish code-mixed dataset to date, containing 125,615 instances and over 376K expert annotations across five core NLP tasks with high inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa >= 0.817).; Closed-weight LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) substantially outperform open-weight models in zero-shot settings on most tasks, whereas traditional specialized tools (codeswitch) remain superior in zero-shot POS tagging.; One-shot in-context learning consistently improves performance across models and tasks, particularly in entity disambiguation and structure-sensitive tasks like NER and MT.; Supervised fine-tuning on COMI-LINGUA enables compact 7-8B open-weight models to match or exceed large proprietary models (e.g., reaching up to 95.25 F1 in NER and 98.77 F1 in MLI).; Qualitative error analysis highlights severe LLM failure modes on code-mixed text, including misclassifying Devanagari-script English borrowings, context truncation on long inputs, output repetition/hallucination, generating Python code snippets instead of task predictions, and prompt mimicry.
Scope and Delimitations: Restricted exclusively to Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-mixed text, filtering out monolingual English/Hindi and other languages.; Covers both Devanagari and Roman scripts across formal (news, press releases) and informal (social media) domains in the Indian subcontinent.; Delimited to five core NLP tasks: Token-level Language Identification (LID), Matrix Language Identification (MLI), Named Entity Recognition (NER), Part-Of-Speech (POS) Tagging, and Machine Translation (MT into English, Romanized Hindi, and Devanagari Hindi).; Requires a Code-Mixing Index (CMI) >= 9 and sentence length >= 5 tokens for raw instance retention.; Empirical evaluation is delimited to traditional toolkits (Microsoft LID, codeswitch), 7B-70B open-weight LLMs, and commercial closed-weight LLMs under zero-shot, one-shot, and LoRA fine-tuning paradigms.
Limitations (Summary): The authors acknowledge four primary limitations: (1) findings are specific to Hindi-English and may not generalize to other code-mixed language pairs with different syntactic or sociolinguistic dynamics; (2) reliance on a small, homogeneous group of three annotators may introduce demographic bias; (3) scaling the curation to other code-mixed pairs is constrained by scarce corpora and robust models; and (4) high computational requirements for fine-tuning may restrict accessibility in resource-constrained environments.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt):
While this study offers valuable insights into the annotation and processing of Hinglish code-mixed text, several limitations warrant consideration:

- 1. Language Pair Specificity: The findings derived from Hinglish code-mixed data may not generalize to other language pairs (e.g., Spanish-English), given differences in syntactic structure, sociolinguistic norms, and code-switching behavior.
- 2. Demographic Bias: The use of a relatively small and homogeneous group of annotators may introduce demographic bias, potentially limiting the broader applicability and reliability of the acceptability ratings.
- 3. Resource Constraints: Scaling this work to other code-mixed language pairs remains challenging due to the scarcity of high-quality annotated corpora and the limited availability of models capable of robustly handling diverse code-mixing phenomena.
- 4. Computational Accessibility: While finetuning shows substantial improvements, computational requirements and the need for substantial training data may limit accessibility for resource-constrained settings.
Generalizability Gap: The dataset and empirical findings are restricted exclusively to Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-mixed text within the Indian subcontinent and may not generalize to other code-mixed language pairs, language families, or sociolinguistic environments. In addition, the small, homogeneous pool of three graduate annotators may limit demographic and dialectal representativeness.
Methodological Gap: The dataset creation workflow relied on automated pre-annotation tools (Microsoft LID, CodeSwitch, LLaMA 3.3) followed by manual post-editing, which introduces potential pre-annotation bias. Furthermore, LLM evaluation was constrained to zero-shot and fixed one-shot prompts without exploring few-shot scaling or chain-of-thought prompting, and parameter fine-tuning was limited to compact 7-8B models due to compute constraints.
Future Work: Scaling dataset curation and annotation frameworks to other under-resourced code-mixed language pairs beyond Hinglish.; Incorporating active learning and iterative refinement pipelines to sustain performance gains and reduce manual annotation overhead.; Expanding annotator demographic diversity to capture wider regional and dialectal language variations.; Developing script-aware and context-sensitive modeling architectures to better handle cross-script borrowed words, mitigate hallucinations, and prevent context truncation in compact LLMs.

Title: Deep multi-task learning: a review of concepts, methods, and cross-domain applications
Authors: Mahmoud Mohamed Abdelsamie; Shahira Shaaban Azab; Hesham A. Hefny
Venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analytics
Domain: Deep learning and multi-task learning across cross-domain applications (natural language processing, computer vision, healthcare, bioinformatics, power systems, robotics, finance, climate science, and physics)
Problem Statement: Providing a comprehensive, unified review and taxonomy of deep multi-task learning (MTL) concepts, architectural sharing mechanisms (hard vs. soft parameter sharing), optimization challenges (negative transfer, task imbalance, hyperparameter sensitivity), and cross-domain application strategies.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-task learning (MTL) inductive transfer bias and shared representation learning; hard and soft parameter sharing paradigms; multi-objective optimization and regularized joint loss formulation
Methodology: Comprehensive literature review and bibliometric quantitative analysis of 6,872 unique Scopus-indexed publications (2020–2025) on multi-task learning, combined with structural taxonomy categorization of MTL architectures (single-domain, multimodal, learned, conditional) and cross-domain application analysis.
Key Findings: MTL publication volume grew rapidly between 2020 and mid-2025, peaking in 2024, with major contributions from computer science (4,698 papers), engineering (1,135 papers), mathematics (498 papers), and medicine/health sciences (241 papers).; Hard parameter sharing shares hidden layers while keeping task-specific heads, providing low computational complexity and reduced overfitting for highly related tasks, whereas soft parameter sharing regularizes separate per-task networks to maintain similarity, offering higher flexibility for loosely related tasks at higher computational cost.; MTL architectures are systematically categorized into single-domain (shared trunk, cross-talk/cross-stitch, prediction distillation, hierarchical/modular/generative), multimodal (e.g., OmniNet), learned (structure search, branched, modular, fine-grained sharing), and conditional architectures.; MTL fundamentally differs from transfer learning: MTL simultaneously learns all tasks using bidirectional knowledge sharing across shared backbones, whereas transfer learning transfers knowledge sequentially and unidirectionally from a source to a target domain.; Primary operational bottlenecks across domains include negative transfer among conflicting tasks, task imbalance during gradient optimization, acute hyperparameter sensitivity, and training scalability constraints with large task counts.
Scope and Delimitations: Focused on deep multi-task learning research published between 2020 and mid-2025 indexed in the Scopus database (articles, conference papers, and review papers).; Restricted subject areas to computer science, engineering, mathematics, physics, medicine, decision sciences, neuroscience, business, and social sciences.; Excluded non-peer-reviewed whitepapers, non-English publications, and purely non-deep traditional statistical multi-task learning methods.
Limitations (Summary): MTL faces negative transfer when tasks conflict, task imbalance where dominant tasks skew gradient updates, elevated architectural complexity across multimodal or heterogeneous tasks, acute hyperparameter sensitivity (task loss weights, learning rates), and severe optimization/memory scalability constraints when scaling to dozens or hundreds of tasks.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Despite its potential benefits, MTL presents several draw-backs and limitations. One major challenge is negative transfer, which occurs when tasks are too different or con-flicting, causing the shared learning process to affect the performance when trained jointly [51, 52, 56]. Task imbalance is another problem, where some tasks may dominate the learning process due to larger datasets, stronger gradients, or simpler objectives, leading to poor performance on low-resource or complex tasks. [53]. Furthermore, Architectural Complexity, designing suit-able architectures that allow for both shared and task-specific components, is non-trivial, especially when tasks differ in modality, structure, or scale [10]. Another one of the most significant limitations of MTL is the sensitivity of hyperparameters. Unlike single-task mod-els, multi-task learning systems often require fine-tuning of various hyperparameters, such as task-specific weights, learning rates, and optimization strategies [94, 95]. This addi-tional layer of complexity can significantly increase the effort required during the model development phase, as finding the optimal balance between tasks is critical to avoid poor performance or negative transfer.
Generalizability Gap: Many domain-specific MTL implementations have only been evaluated on narrow single-language or single-institution benchmarks (e.g., specific Arabic dialects, college student cohorts, discrete robotic action spaces, or constant pressure physical models) without cross-institutional validation or continuous dexterous control environments.
Methodological Gap: Existing MTL methods often rely on empirical trial-and-error or heuristic task weighting; they lack automated mechanisms to eliminate negative transfer, struggle with gradient interference and computational memory bottlenecks at scale, and often lack model interpretability in high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance.
Future Work: Developing dynamic task weighting approaches using attention mechanisms and deep reinforcement learning to adaptively evaluate task contributions during training and mitigate negative transfer.; Integrating meta-learning ('learning to learn') techniques to automatically discover optimal representation sharing strategies and balance shared versus task-specific components.; Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) and foundation models for zero-shot and few-shot multi-task transfer across diverse domains.; Enhancing model interpretability, reliability, and explainability for high-stakes MTL deployments in healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems.; Designing scalable task grouping and optimization frameworks to manage dozens or hundreds of tasks without excessive memory consumption or gradient conflict.

Title: Evaluating Urgency of Typhoon-Related Tweets Through Sentiment Analysis Using Artificial Neural Networks
Authors: Ronnel P. Ermino; Ray Carlo A. Abacan; Nadine Gweneth C. Diamante; Kristine Marie N. Faca; Thatiana Erica D. Juntereal
Venue: International Journal of Computing Sciences Research
Domain: Crisis informatics and disaster management in the Philippines, focusing on social media NLP (Twitter) in English, Tagalog, and bilingual English-Tagalog (Taglish).
Problem Statement: Evaluating the urgency of disaster- and typhoon-related tweets in the Philippines to rapidly identify urgent distress and rescue calls from social media data during and after natural calamities, addressing the operational gap between public social media usage and government emergency response workflows.
Theoretical Framework: Supervised sentiment analysis and crisis communication modeling using a feed-forward artificial neural network to estimate tweet urgency on a continuous scale.
Methodology: A supervised feed-forward artificial neural network (ANN) constructed in Python with TensorFlow. The NLP pipeline involves data collection via Tweepy/Twitter API, text preprocessing (deduplication, lowercasing, non-alphanumeric character removal, tokenization, sequence conversion, and padding to 140 words), an Embedding layer (8,000 vocabulary size, 8 embedding dimensions), a Global Average Pooling 1D layer, a Dense hidden layer (24 units with ReLU activation), and a Dense output layer (1 unit with Sigmoid activation) trained with Binary Cross-Entropy loss.
Datasets and Benchmarks: 4,020 labeled Typhoon Ulysses (Vamco) tweets (2,010 urgent, 2,010 non-urgent) collected from November 8 to November 16, 2020 in English, Tagalog, and Taglish, partitioned into 3,900 training tweets and 120 validation tweets; A separate validation dataset of 100 disaster-related tweets (43 urgent, 57 non-urgent) for confusion matrix analysis
Evaluation and Metrics: training metrics: (accuracy: 0.9987, binary cross entropy loss: 0.0074); simultaneous validation metrics: (dataset size: 120, accuracy: 0.9917, binary cross entropy loss: 0.068); confusion matrix validation metrics: (dataset size: 100, true positives: 42, true negatives: 57, false positives: 0, false negatives: 1, accuracy: 0.99, sensitivity recall: 0.9767, specificity: 1.0, precision positive predictive value: 1.0, negative predictive value: 0.9828, false positive rate: 0.0, false discovery rate: 0.0, false negative rate: 0.0233, f1 score: 0.9882)
Key Findings: The feed-forward artificial neural network achieved 99.87% accuracy and 0.0074 loss on training, and 99.17% accuracy and 0.0680 loss on simultaneous validation.; Confusion matrix analysis on a separate 100-tweet validation dataset demonstrated 99% accuracy, 97.67% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% precision, 98.28% negative predictive value, and a 98.82% F1 score, with zero false positives and one false negative.; The lightweight architecture with an 8-dimensional embedding layer and global average pooling outperformed prior recurrent neural network baselines (86.99% for standard RNN and 87.6% for bidirectional RNN) on disaster tweet sentiment evaluation.; Continuous urgency scoring via sigmoid activation effectively differentiated high-urgency rescue requests from lower-urgency calamity posts such as donation drives.; The model was successfully exported to Protobuf (.pb), HDF5 (.h5), and JSON formats, enabling lightweight cross-platform deployment across Python and JavaScript/Node.js web applications via TensorFlow.js.
Scope and Delimitations: Restricted data collection exclusively to tweets regarding Typhoon Ulysses (Vamco) between November 8 and November 16, 2020.; Delimited languages to English, Tagalog, and bilingual Taglish.; Fixed maximum tweet sequence length to 140 words and vocabulary size to 8,000 words.; Constrained urgency evaluation to binary supervision (urgent vs. non-urgent) mapped to a continuous 0 to 1 score.; Delimited model architecture to a feed-forward ANN with 8-dimensional embeddings, global average pooling, and one 24-unit ReLU dense layer, excluding recurrent or transformer models.
Limitations (Summary): The model utilizes a small, fixed vocabulary of 8,000 words and was trained on a dataset limited to a single typhoon event (Typhoon Ulysses) in English and Tagalog, which restricts vocabulary coverage, handling of regional Philippine dialects, and out-of-vocabulary terms in unseen disaster scenarios.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Even though the researchers were able to reach a high accuracy using the model and the preprocessed dataset but it is still recommended for future researchers to expand the vocabulary of the embedding layer by adding more diverse data to the dataset, even more so if the model will process multilingual inputs.
Generalizability Gap: The dataset and evaluation are restricted exclusively to a single typhoon event (Typhoon Ulysses) in the Philippines in November 2020 and limited to English and Tagalog text; generalizability across other natural disaster types (e.g., earthquakes, volcanic eruptions), different typhoon events, other Philippine regional languages (e.g., Cebuano, Ilocano, Waray), and international crisis settings has not been established.
Methodological Gap: The study evaluated model performance on relatively small validation sets (120 simultaneous validation tweets and 100 test tweets) without k-fold cross-validation, out-of-domain testing, or ablation analysis. The model uses static 8-dimensional token embeddings and global average pooling rather than contextual language representations (e.g., RoBERTa or multilingual transformer encoders), and does not leverage metadata (timestamps, retweets, user credibility) or multimodal features (images and videos).
Future Work: Expanding the embedding layer vocabulary and training dataset by collecting more diverse and multilingual disaster data.; Integrating the urgency evaluation model into live disaster incident reporting systems for government agencies and non-governmental organizations.; Implementing real-time tweet stream processing using JavaScript, Node.js, and TensorFlow.js with the exported JSON model format.; Developing Python-based emergency management and rescue applications utilizing the Protobuf (.pb) and HDF5 (.h5) model exports.

Title: GLUECoS: An Evaluation Benchmark for Code-Switched NLP
Authors: Simran Khanuja; Sandipan Dandapat; Anirudh Srinivasan; Sunayana Sitaram; Monojit Choudhury
Venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2020)
Domain: Multilingual Natural Language Processing (NLP), Code-Switching / Code-Mixing across English-Hindi (En-Hi; Roman and Devanagari scripts) and English-Spanish (En-Es; Roman script) from social media, chat, search queries, and conversational transcripts.
Problem Statement: The lack of standardized datasets and comprehensive multi-task evaluation benchmarks for code-switched natural language processing, hindering rigorous comparison across different representation methods (cross-lingual embeddings vs. pre-trained multilingual language models) on varied linguistic tasks.
Theoretical Framework: Linguistic theories of grammatical code-switching (including Equivalence Constraint and Switch Point Fraction for synthetic generation) alongside quantitative code-mixing metrics (Code-Mixing Index [CMI], Switch-Point Average [SP Avg], Multilingual Index [M-index], Probability of Switching [I-index], Burstiness, Language Entropy [LE], and Span Entropy [SE]).
Methodology: The authors introduce GLUECoS, a standardized evaluation benchmark spanning six NLP tasks (Language Identification, Part-of-Speech Tagging, Named Entity Recognition, Sentiment Analysis, Question Answering, and a newly curated conversational Natural Language Inference task) across English-Hindi and English-Spanish. They standardize datasets into balanced 8:1:1 train:dev:test splits and evaluate five representation paradigms: (1) baseline monolingual word embeddings, (2) cross-lingual embeddings (unsupervised and supervised MUSE, BiCVM, BiSkip), (3) synthetic code-switched skip-gram embeddings (GCM), (4) pre-trained Multilingual BERT (mBERT), and (5) Modified mBERT fine-tuned via masked language modeling on a curriculum of synthetic code-switched data (gCM) followed by real code-switched data (rCM). Tasks are evaluated using task-specific architectures including BiLSTM-CRF for word-level sequence labeling, BiLSTM for sentence classification, and BiDAF/Transformers for QA and NLI.
Datasets and Benchmarks: FIRE 2013 (FIRE LID) - English-Hindi word-level Language Identification (Devanagari script; 3,537 sentences); EMNLP 2014 - English-Spanish word-level Language Identification (14,413 sentences); UD POS (Bhat et al., 2018) - English-Hindi Universal Dependency POS tagging (Devanagari script; 1,814 sentences); FG POS (ICON 2016 / Jamatia et al., 2016) - English-Hindi fine-grained POS tagging (Roman script; 2,631 sentences); Bangor Miami Corpus (Bangor POS) - English-Spanish POS tagging (2,758 sentences); IIITH NER (Singh et al., 2018) - English-Hindi Twitter Named Entity Recognition (Roman script; 3,084 sentences); CALCS 2018 (Aguilar et al., 2019) - English-Spanish Twitter Named Entity Recognition (34,208 sentences); SAIL 2017 (Patra et al., 2018) - English-Hindi social media Sentiment Analysis (Roman script; 12,601 sentences); Vilares et al. (2016) - English-Spanish Twitter Sentiment Analysis (2,103 sentences); Chandu et al. (2018a) / DrQA - English-Hindi Question Answering (313 question-answer-context triples); Khanuja et al. (2020) - English-Hindi Conversational Natural Language Inference (Roman script; 1,300 sentence pairs); Pre-training Corpora: IIT Bombay English-Hindi parallel corpus (10M GCM / 2M gCM), Twitter English-Spanish parallel corpus (4.5M), Pratapa et al. (2018a) English-Spanish synthetic corpus (8M), Chandu et al. (2018b) En-Hi real code-mixed corpus (93k), Rijhwani et al. (2017) En-Es real code-mixed corpus (93k)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: Token-level F1 for LID, NER, and Sentiment Analysis; F1 and Accuracy for POS tagging; F1 for QA; Accuracy for NLI; lid performance: Modified mBERT achieves top performance (FIRE En-Hi F1: 96.60 vs mBERT 95.87, Sup MUSE 94.92; EMNLP En-Es F1: 96.24 vs mBERT 95.97, Sup MUSE 93.39); pos tagging performance: Modified mBERT achieves top results among embedding methods (UD En-Hi F1: 88.06 vs mBERT 87.16, SOTA 90.53; Bangor En-Es F1: 93.62 vs mBERT 93.33, SOTA 95.39; FG En-Hi F1: 63.31 vs mBERT 63.42, SOTA 80.80); ner performance: Modified mBERT significantly outperforms baseline and cross-lingual models (IIITH En-Hi F1: 78.21 vs mBERT 74.96, baseline 71.52; CALCS En-Es F1: 61.77 vs mBERT 59.69, baseline 47.90); sentiment analysis performance: Modified mBERT reaches highest F1 scores (SAIL En-Hi F1: 59.35 vs mBERT 58.24, baseline 50.44; En-Es Sentiment F1: 69.31 vs mBERT 66.03, baseline 50.62); qa and nli performance: mBERT achieves highest score on En-Hi QA (F1: 71.96 vs Modified mBERT 68.01, BiSkip 65.56); on Conversational NLI, Modified mBERT outperforms standard mBERT but both perform only slightly above chance
Key Findings: Pre-trained multilingual contextual language models (mBERT) significantly outperform static cross-lingual word embedding techniques (MUSE, BiCVM, BiSkip) across all evaluated code-switching tasks and language pairs.; Fine-tuning mBERT on synthetically generated code-switched data (gCM) paired with a small portion (<5%) of real code-mixed text (rCM) on masked language modeling further improves downstream performance across most tasks.; Models consistently perform better on English-Spanish than English-Hindi, reflecting syntactic similarities between English and Spanish (word order preservation), the absence of script variation noise, and higher domain alignment in training data.; Word-level tasks like Language Identification (F1 > 96%) and POS tagging are relatively tractable, whereas semantic and discourse-level reasoning tasks (QA and NLI) remain far from solved, with NLI performance hovering near chance levels.; Static cross-lingual word embeddings underperform in code-switched contexts because bilingual lexicon induction objectives fail to model the non-linear semantic and distributional shifts characteristic of mixed discourse.
Scope and Delimitations: Restricted to two code-switched language pairs: English-Hindi (typologically distinct language family with script variation) and English-Spanish (typologically closer pair in Roman script).; Delimited to six specific NLP tasks: Language Identification (LID), Part-of-Speech (POS) Tagging, Named Entity Recognition (NER), Sentiment Analysis, Question Answering (QA), and Natural Language Inference (NLI).; Focuses strictly on textual modalities (social media, microblogs, chats, and Wikipedia text), excluding spoken code-switching.; Evaluates models in individual task setups rather than a joint multi-task learning architecture.; Employs synthetic code-switching generation using linguistic constraints (Switch Point Fraction) for pre-training, supplemented with less than 5% real code-switched data.
Limitations (Summary): The authors acknowledge several major limitations: (1) direct comparison between cross-lingual word embeddings and mBERT is confounded by large differences in training data scale and pre-training domains (social media/query logs vs. Wikipedia dump); (2) performance on English-Hindi is hindered by non-standard Romanized spelling, transliterator errors, syntactic differences in word order, and generic pre-training data; (3) evaluation is conducted on single-task pipelines rather than a multi-task learning framework; and (4) performance on complex semantic reasoning tasks like NLI and Sentiment Analysis remains low, demonstrating that current models do not yet truly understand code-switched language.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt):
The results using mBERT cannot be directly compared to the cross-lingual models because of the difference in the magnitude of data involved in training. Also, due to the fact that mBERT is trained on 104 languages together, with massive amounts of data for a large number of epochs, it learns several common features better providing for a well represented common embedding space. The training data used for training the cross-lingual embeddings is restricted to Twitter and query logs, while mBERT is trained on the entire wiki dump.

Overall, the cross-lingual and mBERT models perform better for *English-Spanish* as compared to *English-Hindi*. This could be due to several reasons.

- English and Spanish are similar languages, with both mostly retaining individual word order while code-switching, which is not the case for English and Hindi.
- Romanized Hindi does not use standardized spellings, and errors made by the transliterator could have influenced the results.
- We use Twitter and social media data to train cross lingual word embeddings for *English-Spanish* which are similar in domain to the task datasets, while we use the IITB and query-based parallel corpora for *English-Hindi* which is generic in domain, constrained by the available resources at hand.

We find that accuracies vary across tasks in the GLUECoS benchmark, and except in the case of LID, code-switched NLP is far from solved. This is particularly stark in the case of Sentiment and NLI, which are three and two way classification tasks respectively. Modified mBERT performs only a little over chance, which shows that we are still in the early days of solving NLI for code-switched languages, and also indicates that our models are far from truly being able to understand code-switched language.
Generalizability Gap: The benchmark is limited to only two language pairs (English-Hindi and English-Spanish) in written social media and conversational domains. It leaves unexamined other code-switched language families (e.g., non-Indo-European pairs, low-resource African or Southeast Asian languages), spoken code-switching contexts, and domains beyond social media and chat.
Methodological Gap: The benchmark evaluates models on isolated tasks using standard task-specific heads rather than utilizing a unified multi-task learning architecture to facilitate cross-task transfer for data-scarce code-switched tasks. Additionally, processing Romanized Hindi relies on external off-the-shelf transliteration and language identification tools rather than end-to-end normalization.
Future Work: Implementing and benchmarking models in a multi-task learning setup to allow data-scarce code-switched tasks to benefit from resource-rich tasks.; Adding more diverse tasks and language pairs to subsequent versions of the GLUECoS benchmark.; Pre-training dedicated language models from scratch on code-switched and constituent monolingual corpora rather than solely fine-tuning pre-existing multilingual models.; Releasing the new code-switched conversational Natural Language Inference (NLI) dataset for broader research community use.
