Title: Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning
Authors: Tianhe Yu; Saurabh Kumar; Abhishek Gupta; Sergey Levine; Karol Hausman; Chelsea Finn
Venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020)
Domain: Multi-Task Supervised Learning and Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning
Problem Statement: Multi-task learning frequently suffers from severe optimization failures where joint training performs worse than independent single-task training because task gradients conflict with one another under high curvature and disparate gradient magnitudes.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-objective optimization and gradient dynamics under the tragic triad condition, establishing convergence for convex Lipschitz objectives and proving local loss improvement conditions for orthogonal gradient projection.
Methodology: Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) deconflicts task gradients by projecting each task gradient onto the normal plane of any conflicting task gradient with negative cosine similarity. The algorithm computes gradients for each task minibatch, iterates through all other tasks in random order, subtracts the projected component along conflicting gradients, and sums the resulting modified gradients to update shared network parameters.
Datasets and Benchmarks: MultiMNIST (multi-task digit classification dataset); Cityscapes (urban scene understanding benchmark); CelebA (200,000 celebrity face images with 40 binary attribute classification tasks); Multi-task CIFAR-100 (20 coarse-class classification tasks with 2,500 training and 500 testing instances per task); NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding dataset with 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction); Meta-World MT10 (robotic manipulation benchmark with 10 distinct manipulation tasks); Meta-World MT50 (robotic manipulation benchmark with 50 distinct manipulation tasks); Goal-conditioned RL environments (2D navigation and Fetch robotic manipulation domains)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Top-1 classification accuracy (%) for Multi-task CIFAR-100; Average binary classification error (%) across 40 attribute tasks for CelebA; Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and pixel accuracy for NYUv2 semantic segmentation; Absolute error and relative error for NYUv2 depth estimation; Mean angle distance, median angle distance, and percentage of pixels within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for NYUv2 surface normal prediction; Task success rate (%) and sample efficiency (million environment steps) for Meta-World MT10 and MT50 reinforcement learning benchmarks]; baselines: [Vanilla multi-task gradient descent (equal loss weights with Adam or SGD); Independent single-task learning models; Multi-Task Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Multi-Head SAC; Cross-Stitch Networks (Misra et al., 2016); Routing Networks with Weak Positive Localization (Rosenbaum et al., 2018); Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN, Liu et al., 2018); Uncertainty Weighting (Kendall et al., 2018); Dynamic Weight Average (DWA, Liu et al., 2018); Multiple-Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA, Sener & Koltun, 2018); GradNorm (Chen et al., 2018); Cosine Similarity Regularization (Suteu & Guo, 2019)]; architectures: [Convolutional neural network trunk for CelebA multi-label classification; Routing network architecture with fully connected modules for CIFAR-100; Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) with SegNet backbone for NYUv2; Multi-layer perceptron actor and critic networks in Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) for Meta-World RL]
Key Findings: PCGrad significantly improves optimization stability, data efficiency, and asymptotic performance across multi-task supervised learning and reinforcement learning domains by eliminating destructive gradient interference.; On CIFAR-100 multi-task classification, PCGrad on a single network achieves 71.0% accuracy, surpassing independent training (67.7%) and cross-stitch networks (53.0%). Combining PCGrad with routing networks achieves 77.5% accuracy, which adds a 2.8% absolute gain over routing networks alone.; On the CelebA 40-task attribute prediction benchmark, PCGrad reduces average classification error to 8.69%, outperforming the multi-objective optimization baseline by Sener and Koltun (8.95%).; On the NYUv2 multi-task benchmark, combining MTAN with PCGrad achieves superior results across 8 out of 9 evaluation metrics across semantic segmentation (20.17 mIoU), depth estimation (0.5904 absolute error), and surface normal prediction.; On Meta-World MT10, PCGrad with SAC successfully solves all 10 robotic manipulation tasks (100% success rate) while saving 2 million environment samples compared to independent SAC models, whereas vanilla multi-task SAC fails to solve half of the tasks.; On Meta-World MT50, PCGrad with SAC learns approximately 70% of the 50 manipulation tasks, matching independent training while reducing sample requirements by 15 million environment transitions.; Ablation studies confirm that altering both gradient directions and gradient magnitudes is essential because altering only gradient directions or only gradient magnitudes degrades multi-task performance substantially.
Scope and Delimitations: Evaluates gradient projection on shared network parameters in multi-task supervised learning, multi-task reinforcement learning, and goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.; Requires individual per-task gradient computations for all tasks present within each training minibatch prior to applying gradient projection.; Implements pairwise sequential gradient projections using a randomized task ordering rather than computing simultaneous multi-gradient quadratic programming solutions.; Focuses on multi-task settings where task identity metadata or task conditioning vectors are available during training.
Limitations (Summary): The theoretical convergence of PCGrad can stall or yield sub-optimal parameters if task gradients exhibit exact opposite alignment (cosine similarity of -1), which causes zero gradient updates. In addition, computing separate backward passes for every task in a minibatch introduces computational and memory overhead as the task count increases.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): A sub-optimal solution occurs when the cosine similarity between the gradients of the two tasks is exactly −1, i.e. the gradients directly conflict, leading to zero gradient after applying PCGrad. However, in practice, since we are using SGD, which is a noisy estimate of the true batch gradients, the cosine similarity between the gradients of two tasks in a minibatch is unlikely to be −1, thus avoiding this scenario. Note that, in theory, convergence may be slow if cos(φ12) hovers near −1.
Generalizability Gap: The authors evaluated PCGrad on computer vision image datasets and simulated robotic manipulation benchmarks; the authors did not test the algorithm on large-scale natural language processing models, real-world physical robotic platforms, generative models, or multi-agent environments.
Methodological Gap: PCGrad computes task projections sequentially based on a random task order rather than solving a joint multi-task optimization problem, which introduces order-dependent variance; furthermore, computing individual backward passes for each task scales computational complexity linearly with the number of tasks in each minibatch.
Future Work: Applying PCGrad to meta-learning, continual lifelong learning, multi-goal imitation learning, and natural language processing tasks.; Extending gradient surgery principles to stabilize broader machine learning settings such as two-player games and multi-agent optimization.; Designing robust and safe multi-task reinforcement learning algorithms to mitigate unsafe exploration behaviors.; Developing self-supervised and unsupervised multi-task reinforcement learning methods to overcome reward specification challenges on physical robotic systems.

Title: GradNorm: Gradient Normalization for Adaptive Loss Balancing in Deep Multitask Networks
Authors: Zhao Chen; Vijay Badrinarayanan; Chen-Yu Lee; Andrew Rabinovich
Venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
Domain: Computer Vision and Deep Multitask Learning
Problem Statement: Deep multitask neural networks frequently suffer from poor training dynamics because different tasks exhibit disparate loss scales and learning speeds, which produces severe gradient magnitude imbalances across shared parameters and causes dominant tasks to suppress the learning of other tasks.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-task optimization and gradient dynamics, based on the principle that optimal multi-task representation sharing requires balancing task learning rates by scaling gradient norms proportionally to relative inverse training speeds.
Methodology: GradNorm dynamically balances multitask training by tuning task loss weights w_i(t) at each step to equalize task training rates. The algorithm measures the L2 gradient norm G_W^(i)(t) of each weighted task loss at the final shared layer W, determines target gradient norms G_W(t) * [r_i(t)]^alpha based on the average gradient norm across tasks and the relative inverse training rate r_i(t) = (L_i(t)/L_i(0)) / E[L_j(t)/L_j(0)], updates weights w_i(t) via gradient descent on an L1 loss L_grad between actual and target gradient norms, and renormalizes task weights to sum to the total number of tasks T.
Datasets and Benchmarks: Synthetic Multi-Task Regression Dataset (Toy 2-task and 10-task non-linear regression problems with varied task loss scales); NYUv2+seg (NYU Depth V2 dataset with 795 training and 654 test indoor images annotated for depth, surface normals, and 13-class semantic segmentation); NYUv2+kpts (Augmented NYU Depth V2 dataset with 90,000 indoor images annotated for depth, surface normals, and 48 room keypoint types); 9-task Facial Landmark Dataset (Supplementary multi-task facial benchmark)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Task-normalized test-time loss (sum of test loss ratios relative to initial loss); Root Mean Square Error (RMS in meters) for depth estimation; 100 - Mean Intersection over Union (100 - IoU) for semantic segmentation error; Cosine distance (1 - cos theta) for surface normal error; Percentage pixel error (%) for room keypoint layout prediction; L2 parameter distance to optimal static weights]; baselines: [Single-task networks (dedicated single-task models); Equal weights baseline (static w_i = 1 for all tasks); GradNorm Static (static weights set to time-averaged weights from a dynamic GradNorm run); Uncertainty weighting baseline (Kendall et al., 2017); Exhaustive random grid search (100 multi-task networks trained with uniformly sampled weights)]; architectures: [4-layer fully connected trunk for synthetic regression; VGG-16 SegNet encoder-decoder (29M parameters); Modified thin ResNet-50 FCN (15M parameters)]
Key Findings: GradNorm improves multi-task test performance across regression and classification tasks, outperforming single-task models, equal weights baselines, and uncertainty weighting baselines.; On NYUv2+seg with a VGG-16 backbone, GradNorm with alpha = 1.5 achieves 0.925m depth RMS error, 67.8 segmentation error, and 0.174 normals error, surpassing the equal weights baseline (0.944m, 70.1, 0.192).; On NYUv2+kpts, GradNorm reduces depth error to 0.629m, keypoint error to 7.73%, and normals error to 0.139, outperforming both single-task networks and adaptive uncertainty weighting.; GradNorm provides effective regularization by preventing fast-learning tasks from overfitting, which allows tasks such as depth estimation to achieve lower test error despite converging to higher training loss.; A single GradNorm training run identifies task weights that match or surpass the performance of 100-run exhaustive grid searches, drastically reducing hyperparameter tuning computation.; The asymmetry hyperparameter alpha controls balancing intensity, where low values (e.g., alpha = 0.12) suit symmetric tasks and higher values (e.g., alpha = 1.5) effectively stabilize highly asymmetric multi-task learning dynamics.
Scope and Delimitations: Applied gradient normalization specifically to the final shared layer of weights W to restrict computational overhead to approximately 5%.; Constrained loss weighting to linear combinations of single-task losses subject to the normalization constraint sum(w_i(t)) = T.; Evaluated primarily on computer vision problems comprising simultaneous dense prediction tasks (depth, normals, segmentation, and keypoint heatmaps) with fixed input resolutions of 320x320 and output resolutions of 80x80.; Assumed model architectures with shared trunks and task-specific heads rather than branched or cross-talk architectures.
Limitations (Summary): The authors acknowledge that no general scalar metric exists to evaluate multitask performance objectively across diverse task combinations with different loss scales. Additionally, GradNorm adds gradient compute overhead (~5%), relies on stable initial loss values L_i(0), and balances gradients only at a single shared layer.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): There unfortunately exists no general single scalar which gives a meaningful measure of multitask performance in all scenarios, but our toy problem was specifically designed with tasks which are statistically identical except for their loss scales σ i .
Generalizability Gap: The proposed method was evaluated exclusively on computer vision datasets (NYUv2 and facial landmarks) and synthetic multi-output regressions; the authors did not test the algorithm on other machine learning domains such as natural language processing, speech synthesis, reinforcement learning, or multi-modal foundation models.
Methodological Gap: GradNorm computes gradient norms solely at the final shared layer W rather than across intermediate backbone layers, which may not resolve gradient conflicts occurring in earlier shared layers; furthermore, the method requires an empirical hyperparameter alpha and depends on stable initial loss values L_i(0) to compute relative training rates.
Future Work: Extending the GradNorm gradient balancing formulation to class-imbalanced classification problems.; Applying GradNorm to sequence-to-sequence models and language processing tasks with conflicting gradient updates.; Investigating gradient manipulation algorithms in other complex architectures and non-vision multi-objective learning settings.

Title: Humaid-Ner: A Disaster Tweet Dataset for Joint Named Entity Recognition and Event Classification Via Uncertainty-Weighted Multitask Learning
Authors: Aijaz Ali; Nazish Basir; Sarfaraz Nawaz; Danish Nazir Arain; Haris Ali
Venue: The Asian Bulletin of Big Data Management
Domain: Crisis Informatics, Disaster Response, Social Media NLP (Twitter/X Disaster Tweets in English), Multitask Learning, Named Entity Recognition
Problem Statement: Disaster-related social media benchmarks provide document-level category annotations but lack span-level entity labels (such as location, casualties, displaced counts, or requested supplies) required for operational humanitarian response coordination. Additionally, joint multi-task training of dense token-level named entity recognition and single sentence-level event classification leads to severe gradient asymmetry and task conflict (2,688 NER token signals vs. 1 classification signal per example), causing classification macro-F1 to progressively degrade under fixed-weight multi-task learning.
Theoretical Framework: Homoscedastic uncertainty-based multi-task loss weighting (Kendall et al., 2018) derived from a probabilistic log-likelihood formulation with learnable task variance parameters, coupled with the hierarchical representation learning hypothesis (Liu et al., 2019 / MT-DNN) positing that lower transformer layers capture universal linguistic representations while upper layers encode task-specific patterns.
Methodology: Constructed the HUMAID-NER dataset by extending 60,000 English tweets from the HumAID benchmark across 19 disaster events into 10 operationally motivated entity types (yielding 21 BIO classes) via a three-stage hybrid auto-labelling pipeline combining a spaCy transformer backbone (en_core_web_trf), domain-specific EntityRuler patterns, and regular expressions with priority- and length-based overlap resolution. Designed a joint multitask architecture using a shared RoBERTa-large encoder (24 layers, 355M parameters) with a linear token projection head for sequence labeling and a dual-pooled classification head concatenating the [CLS] embedding and mean non-padding token representations (2,048 dimensions). Trained the model using homoscedastic uncertainty loss weighting with learnable task log-variance parameters (s_NER, s_CLS) and a two-stage training schedule: Stage 1 (epochs 1–7) jointly trains all 24 encoder layers; Stage 2 (epochs 8–15) freezes the bottom 18 layers (reducing active parameters from 355M to 47M) to specialize upper layers and task heads. Developed and deployed a real-time web dashboard for simultaneous single-forward-pass inference.
Datasets and Benchmarks: HUMAID-NER (60,000 English tweets from 19 natural disaster events between 2016 and 2019 sampled from HumAID, annotated with ~175,000 entity spans across 10 disaster-specific types in BIO format; partitioned into 72% train [43,200 tweets], 14% validation [8,400 tweets], and 14% test [8,400 tweets] stratified by 10 humanitarian categories); HumAID benchmark (77,637 English tweets from 19 natural disaster events labelled across 10 humanitarian categories)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Entity-level span micro-F1 via seqeval (exact entity type and span boundary match required); Macro-averaged F1 across 10 humanitarian categories for event classification; Balanced validation combined score: Score_val = 0.5 * F1_NER + 0.5 * F1_CLS; Classification-first deployment policy (prioritizing classification macro-F1 with combined score breaking ties)]; ablation results: (Row A (BERT-large + Fixed Weights): {'NER_span_micro_F1': 0.873, 'CLS_macro_F1': 0.736, 'combined_score': 0.805}, Row B (RoBERTa-large + Fixed Weights): {'NER_span_micro_F1': 0.863, 'CLS_macro_F1': 0.749, 'combined_score': 0.806}, Row C (RoBERTa-large + Kendall Weighting): {'NER_span_micro_F1': 0.866, 'CLS_macro_F1': 0.745, 'combined_score': 0.806}, Row D (RoBERTa-large + Kendall + Two-Stage / Proposed): {'NER_span_micro_F1': 0.841, 'CLS_macro_F1': 0.761, 'combined_score': 0.801}); benchmark comparisons: (HumAID BERT-base (Single-task): {'NER_F1': None, 'CLS_F1': '0.700 - 0.730'}, HumAID RoBERTa-large (Single-task): {'NER_F1': None, 'CLS_F1': '0.730 - 0.750'}, Proposed Joint RoBERTa-large (Row D): {'NER_F1': 0.841, 'CLS_F1': 0.761})
Key Findings: Introduced HUMAID-NER, the first disaster-domain named entity recognition dataset extending HumAID with 60,000 tweets and ~175,000 entity spans across 10 operational entity types (LOCATION, CASUALTY, DISPLACED, REQUEST, RESOURCE, RESCUE, DISASTER_TYPE, ORGANIZATION, PERSON, NUMBER) mapped to 21 BIO classes.; Empirically identified task conflict and gradient asymmetry under fixed-weight joint training, where dense token-level NER supervision (up to 2,688 signals/sample) dominated sentence-level classification (1 signal/sample), causing classification macro-F1 to peak at epoch 3 (0.748) and degrade by 1.4 points to 0.734 by epoch 15 despite monotonic reduction in training loss.; Demonstrated that Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting dynamically balances task losses via learnable log-variance parameters, preventing classification degradation and stabilizing multitask training dynamics.; Found that two-stage layer-freezing training (freezing layers 1–18 in Stage 2) produced the largest classification gain (+1.6 macro-F1 points, reaching 0.761) by reducing active parameters from 355M to 47M and enabling task-head and upper-layer specialization without eroding shared representations.; The proposed joint RoBERTa-large framework achieved 0.841 NER span micro-F1 and 0.761 classification macro-F1 concurrently on the validation split, matching or exceeding single-task RoBERTa-large baselines (0.730–0.750) without incurring classification performance penalties while delivering full entity extraction capabilities.; Demonstrated operational viability via a real-time web dashboard capable of extracting typed entity spans and predicting humanitarian event categories simultaneously in a single forward pass without task-specific inference latency overhead.
Scope and Delimitations: Text corpus restricted to English-language disaster tweets sampled from 19 natural disaster events between 2016 and 2019 in the HumAID benchmark.; Dataset size delimited to a balanced 60,000-tweet subset across 10 humanitarian categories rather than the complete 77,637 HumAID corpus.; Entity taxonomy delimited to 10 operationally motivated humanitarian entity types (21 BIO classes) excluding generic newswire categories.; Empirical evaluation delimited to the held-out validation split (8,400 tweets) to intentionally reserve the test set against overfitting.; Hardware constraints on TPU v3-8 restricted experimental ablations to single-run point estimates without multi-seed variance analysis.
Limitations (Summary): The dataset relies on an automated three-stage hybrid labelling pipeline without human inter-annotator agreement verification; the corpus is restricted to English tweets from 2016–2019 across a 60,000-tweet subset; evaluation reports only validation split results with test set evaluation reserved; ablations are single-run point estimates lacking multi-seed variance analysis due to TPU compute limits; and direct empirical gradient conflict diagnostics were not collected.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Limitations include no human inter-annotator validation of the auto-labelled annotations, English-only coverage (2016–2019), validation-split-only reporting (testset evaluation reserved to prevent overfitting), and single-run point estimates for all ablation results (multi-seed variance analysis was precluded by TPU compute budget and is left for future work).
Generalizability Gap: The dataset and joint framework are limited to English-language tweets from 19 natural disaster events (2016–2019), leaving unexamined non-English and multilingual disaster communications, low-resource regional dialects, multimodal crisis streams (paired text and imagery), and non-natural disaster domains such as industrial accidents, armed conflicts, or public health emergencies.
Methodological Gap: The auto-labelling pipeline lacks formal human inter-annotator agreement metrics (such as Cohen's or Fleiss' Kappa) to quantify pseudo-label noise; direct gradient diagnostics (such as gradient cosine similarity or conflicting gradient norm tracking across shared layers) were not measured to provide direct mechanistic proof of gradient interference; and the ablation study lacks multi-seed statistical variance bounds.
Future Work: Combine PCGrad gradient surgery with Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting to eliminate destructive gradient interference without excessive computational overhead.; Scale the three-stage auto-annotation pipeline to annotate the remaining tweets in the full 77,637-tweet HumAID corpus and new disaster events.; Extend the joint multitask architecture to multilingual crisis tweet analysis using XLM-RoBERTa paired with soft gazetteers.; Conduct direct empirical gradient tracking across encoder layers during multitask training to evaluate gradient conflict dynamics.; Perform multi-seed variance analysis across all model configurations to establish statistical significance bounds.

Title: HumAID: Human-Annotated Disaster Incidents Data from Twitter with Deep Learning Benchmarks
Authors: Firoj Alam; Umair Qazi; Muhammad Imran; Ferda Ofli
Venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2021)
Domain: Crisis Informatics, Natural Language Processing, Disaster Response and Management, Social Media Text Classification
Problem Statement: Social media streams generated during disaster events provide time-critical situational information for emergency response, but raw microblog posts contain high volumes of noise, redundancy, and irrelevant content. Existing crisis informatics datasets suffer from small event scales, exact and near-duplicate messages, lack of location-based filtering for impacted zones, and absent standardized test splits, which prevents researchers from rigorously training and benchmarking modern data-hungry deep learning models for humanitarian disaster management.
Theoretical Framework: Crisis informatics taxonomy and humanitarian information requirements grounded in the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UN OCHA) Multi-Cluster/Sector Initial Rapid Assessment (MIRA) framework, situational awareness theory in emergency response, and inter-coder reliability theory (Fleiss' kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, and majority agreement metrics).
Methodology: The authors created a standardized data collection, filtering, crowdsourcing, and benchmarking pipeline comprising: (1) streaming keyword and hashtag data collection through the AIDR platform across 19 major disaster events (2016–2019) capturing 24,859,155 raw tweets; (2) a multi-stage filtering pipeline incorporating event date bounding, geographic filtering (prioritizing GPS coordinates, followed by place bounding boxes, and OpenStreetMap/Nominatim user profile geocoding), English language filtering, classifier-based pre-filtering with a Random Forest model (F1 = 76.9%) to prune non-humanitarian messages, minimum token length thresholds (greater than or equal to three words or hashtags), and cosine similarity de-duplication on uni-gram and bi-gram term-frequency vectors (threshold 0.75) reducing the collection to 337,082 candidate tweets; (3) class-balanced random sampling yielding 109,612 tweets for annotation; (4) crowdsourced Amazon Mechanical Turk annotation with 10-tweet qualification tests, embedded gold standard check tweets in 30-tweet HITs (requiring at least 70% accuracy), and a 66% inter-annotator consensus threshold across 11 humanitarian categories yielding 77,196 agreed labeled tweets; and (5) supervised multiclass classification benchmarking across event-level, event-type-level, and all-combined splits (70% train, 10% development, 20% test) comparing classical algorithms (Random Forest and Support Vector Machines with TF-IDF n-gram features) against deep learning architectures (fastText, BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa, and XLM-RoBERTa).
Datasets and Benchmarks: HumAID: 77,196 human-annotated English tweets (76,484 tweets utilized in benchmark classification tasks across 10 humanitarian categories after pruning low-prevalence classes with fewer than 15 samples) covering 19 natural disaster events across four disaster types (earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes/cyclones) between 2016 and 2019; AIDR 24.8M Raw Disaster Tweet Stream: 24,859,155 raw tweets collected via Twitter Streaming API across 19 disaster events; Pre-trained fastText Common Crawl Word Embeddings; Pre-trained Transformer Checkpoints: BERT (bert-base-uncased), DistilBERT (distilbert-base-uncased), RoBERTa (roberta-base), and XLM-RoBERTa (xlm-roberta-base)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Weighted Average Precision (P); Weighted Average Recall (R); Weighted Average F1-Measure (F1); Fleiss' Kappa (κ); Krippendorff's Alpha (K-α); Average Observed Agreement (Avg obs.); Average Majority Agreement (Maj agr.)]; inter annotator agreement: (fleiss kappa mean: 0.55, krippendorff alpha mean: 0.57, average observed agreement mean: 0.64, average majority agreement mean: 0.83, range observed agreement: 55% to 83%); benchmark results weighted f1 averages: (RoBERTa (Best Overall): 0.781, XLM-RoBERTa: 0.777, DistilBERT: 0.769, BERT: 0.768, fastText: 0.712, SVM: 0.71, Random Forest: 0.7); benchmark results by event type weighted f1: (Earthquake (9 classes): {'Random_Forest': 0.766, 'SVM': 0.783, 'fastText': 0.789, 'BERT': 0.833, 'DistilBERT': 0.839, 'RoBERTa': 0.836, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.837}, Fire (10 classes): {'Random_Forest': 0.685, 'SVM': 0.717, 'fastText': 0.727, 'BERT': 0.771, 'DistilBERT': 0.771, 'RoBERTa': 0.787, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.779}, Flood (10 classes): {'Random_Forest': 0.653, 'SVM': 0.693, 'fastText': 0.704, 'BERT': 0.749, 'DistilBERT': 0.734, 'RoBERTa': 0.758, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.755}, Hurricane (10 classes): {'Random_Forest': 0.702, 'SVM': 0.716, 'fastText': 0.73, 'BERT': 0.74, 'DistilBERT': 0.742, 'RoBERTa': 0.741, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.739}, Combined All (10 classes): {'Random_Forest': 0.707, 'SVM': 0.731, 'fastText': 0.744, 'BERT': 0.758, 'DistilBERT': 0.758, 'RoBERTa': 0.76, 'XLM-RoBERTa': 0.758})
Key Findings: Transformer-based pretrained language models consistently outperform classical machine learning algorithms (Random Forest and Support Vector Machines) and fastText across individual disaster events, disaster event types, and the combined dataset.; Monolingual RoBERTa achieved the highest overall average performance with a weighted F1-score of 0.781, outperforming XLM-RoBERTa (0.777), DistilBERT (0.769), BERT (0.768), fastText (0.712), SVM (0.710), and Random Forest (0.700).; DistilBERT achieved classification performance comparable to BERT (average weighted F1 of 0.769 compared to 0.768) while operating with substantially fewer parameters and lower computational overhead, establishing DistilBERT as an effective architecture for latency-sensitive operational deployment.; Monolingual pretraining in RoBERTa yielded higher performance on English disaster tweets than multilingual pretraining in XLM-RoBERTa, although XLM-RoBERTa demonstrated strong competitive capability across all disaster categories.; Support Vector Machines outperformed Random Forest across almost all event configurations (0.710 versus 0.700 average weighted F1), demonstrating competitive performance relative to fastText (0.712 weighted F1).; The systematic filtering pipeline (date boundaries, geographic resolution, relevance pre-filtering, token length pruning, and cosine similarity de-duplication) successfully eliminated redundant noise and out-of-area chatter from 24.8 million tweets, yielding moderate to substantial inter-annotator agreement (average Fleiss' kappa of 0.55, Krippendorff's alpha of 0.57, and majority agreement of 0.83).
Scope and Delimitations: The corpus is delimited strictly to English-language tweets collected from the Twitter streaming API via the AIDR platform.; The research scope is restricted to 19 sudden-onset natural disaster events occurring between 2016 and 2019 across four disaster categories (earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes/cyclones) that directly affected land and caused major damage.; The annotation framework enforces a single-label mutually exclusive classification task per tweet across 11 predefined humanitarian categories, deliberately omitting multi-label assignments to optimize crowdworker annotation budgets.; Benchmark classification experiments excluded low-prevalence classes containing fewer than 15 samples per event, reducing the experimental benchmark pool from 77,196 tweets to 76,484 tweets across 10 evaluable humanitarian categories.
Limitations (Summary): The authors acknowledge key constraints in their research design: (1) annotation was limited strictly to English-language tweets due to budgetary restrictions, omitting non-English crisis communications; (2) tweets were assigned a single mutually exclusive category despite microblog messages frequently containing multi-faceted situational information; and (3) low-prevalence classes with fewer than 15 instances were removed from specific event evaluation benchmarks.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): We choose to only annotate English tweets due to budget limitations. Therefore, we discard all non-English tweets using the Twitter provided language metadata for a given tweet. It would be interesting to annotate tweets in other languages in future studies. Though multiple labels can be assigned to a tweet, however, we limited it to one category to reduce the annotation efforts.
Generalizability Gap: The dataset and benchmark models focus exclusively on English-language Twitter messages across four types of natural disasters (earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes/cyclones). Consequently, the empirical findings and trained models may not generalize to non-English or code-switched crisis messages, human-induced emergencies (such as industrial accidents, acts of terrorism, or armed conflicts), slow-onset crises (such as droughts or famines), or alternative social media and messaging platforms (such as Facebook, Telegram, WhatsApp, or Sina Weibo).
Methodological Gap: The study employs a mutually exclusive single-label formulation that cannot capture multi-intent disaster messages containing both urgent supply requests and infrastructural damage reports. In addition, geographic filtering relies on user-provided profile metadata for the 98% of tweets lacking GPS coordinates, which introduces potential location noise and geographical selection bias. Furthermore, the pipeline utilizes an automated Random Forest pre-filter that may discard borderline humanitarian messages prior to human crowdsourcing.
Future Work: Annotating disaster tweets in non-English and low-resource languages to broaden linguistic coverage in crisis informatics.; Conducting cross-event and cross-disaster-type transfer learning and domain adaptation experiments using the standardized public benchmark splits.; Developing multimodal classification architectures that jointly analyze disaster tweet text and accompanying crisis imagery.; Extending annotation taxonomies and machine learning architectures to support multi-label crisis classification.; Deploying and evaluating computationally lightweight transformer models, such as DistilBERT, within real-time streaming disaster relief pipelines.

Title: Injecting Imbalance Sensitivity for Multi-Task Learning
Authors: Zhipeng Zhou; Liu Liu; Peilin Zhao; Wei Gong
Venue: Proceedings of the Thirty-Fourth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-2025)
Domain: Multi-Task Supervised Learning (Dense Scene Understanding, Facial Attribute Classification) and Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning (Robotic Manipulation)
Problem Statement: Multi-task learning optimization methods, particularly gradient manipulation approaches, predominantly focus on resolving gradient conflicts while overlooking the critical issue of gradient imbalance and dominance across tasks, which causes Pareto failures and hinders balanced individual task progress even in the absence of conflicts.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-objective optimization and Pareto optimality theory (Pareto dominance, Pareto front, and Pareto stationarity), Lagrangian duality in convex programming under Slater's condition, and gradient dynamics analyzing gradient similarity, imbalance ratios, and conflict-averse properties.
Methodology: IMbalance-sensitive Gradient (IMGrad) descent method injects imbalance sensitivity into optimization-based multi-task learning paradigms by imposing projected norm constraints. The framework incorporates a constraint (g_i^T d - ||g_i||) into the dual objective to encourage the projected norms of the combined gradient d across all tasks to surpass individual task gradient norms. By applying Lagrangian duality and interchanging minimum and maximum operators via Slater's condition, IMGrad derives an analytical objective that balances global convergence and Pareto properties. The balancing weight mu is adaptively determined by cos theta, where theta represents the angle between the mean task gradient g_0 and the MGDA minimum norm gradient g^m. The authors also extend this principle to augment Nash-MTL by adaptively weighting its agreement and bargaining terms.
Datasets and Benchmarks: Cityscapes (urban scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation); NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction); CelebA (large-scale facial attribute dataset with over 200,000 images evaluated across 40 binary attribute classification tasks); Meta-World MT10 (multi-task robotic manipulation reinforcement learning benchmark with 10 distinct manipulation environments); Synthetic two-task toy benchmark (imbalanced two-objective optimization trajectories derived from CAGrad and Nash-MTL settings)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Delta m% (overall relative multi-task degradation/improvement percentage compared to independent single-task reference oracles); Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pixel Accuracy (Pix. Acc.) for semantic segmentation on Cityscapes and NYUv2; Absolute Error (Abs. Err.) and Relative Error (Rel. Err.) for depth estimation on Cityscapes and NYUv2; Mean Angle Error, Median Angle Error, and Percentage of Pixels within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for surface normal prediction on NYUv2; Average classification degradation Delta m% across 40 attribute classification tasks on CelebA; Average task success rate and standard error of the mean (SEM) over 10 random seeds on Meta-World MT10 reinforcement learning; Statistical imbalance ratios, gradient cosine similarities (cos phi_ij), and individual progress ratios r_i(t) = L_i(t) / L_i(0)]; baselines: [Linear Scalarization (LS / naive mean gradient); Independent single-task learning models; Random Loss Weighting (RLW); Dynamic Weight Average (DWA); Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA); Gradient Drop (GradDrop); Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad); Conflict-Averse Gradient descent (CAGrad); Impartial Multi-Task Learning (IMTL); Nash Multi-Task Learning (Nash-MTL); Momentum-based Correction (MoCo); Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization (FAMO); Scale Invariant (SI), Uncertainty Weighting (UW), Single-Task SAC, Multi-Task SAC, Multi-Head SAC, Soft Modularization (SM), CARE]; architectures: [Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) with SegNet backbone for Cityscapes and NYUv2 scene understanding; 9-layer Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) backbone with task-specific linear classification heads for CelebA; Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) multi-layer perceptron architecture for Meta-World MT10 reinforcement learning]
Key Findings: Empirical analysis reveals that gradient imbalance is a more fundamental obstacle in multi-task optimization than gradient conflict, because balanced task gradients converge to global optima despite severe conflicts, whereas imbalanced gradients frequently stall or cause Pareto failures.; Mainstream optimization-based multi-task learning methods (such as PCGrad, CAGrad, and Nash-MTL) experience Pareto failures and imbalanced individual task progress because existing methods lack simultaneous conflict-averse and imbalance-sensitive properties.; On the NYUv2 3-task benchmark, IMGrad achieves a state-of-the-art Delta m% of -4.57% (outperforming Nash-MTL at -4.04% and FAMO at -4.10%), attaining 40.20 mIoU and 66.19% pixel accuracy in segmentation, and 0.52 absolute error in depth estimation.; On the Cityscapes 2-task benchmark, IMGrad attains a Delta m% of 6.61% (substantially improving over CAGrad at 11.58% and outperforming Nash-MTL at 6.82%), with 75.13 mIoU and 0.0128 absolute depth error.; On the CelebA 40-task facial attribute classification benchmark, IMGrad achieves a Delta m% of 1.27%, demonstrating strong scalability across massive task counts and competitive performance alongside FAMO (1.21%).; On the Meta-World MT10 reinforcement learning benchmark, IMGrad improves CAGrad by over 0.10 in success rate, reaching a state-of-the-art success rate of 0.93 ± 0.068 (compared to 0.83 for CAGrad and 0.91 for Nash-MTL).; Ablation and control group experiments demonstrate that selectively gating multi-task optimization based on gradient imbalance ratios yields consistent performance gains across baselines, whereas gating by gradient conflict similarity yields minimal benefit.
Scope and Delimitations: Focuses strictly on optimization-based multi-task learning with shared backbone architectures and gradient manipulation algorithms, excluding architecture-based parameter sharing designs.; Requires individual per-task gradient evaluations at every training iteration to compute gradient similarities and imbalance ratios.; Evaluates empirical performance on standard benchmarks: 2-task and 3-task dense scene understanding (Cityscapes, NYUv2), 40-task image classification (CelebA), and 10-task robotic manipulation (Meta-World MT10).; Utilizes the cosine angle cos theta between the average task gradient g_0 and the MGDA minimum norm gradient g^m as the primary operational proxy for quantifying gradient imbalance.
Limitations (Summary): The authors acknowledge that IMGrad does not obtain the top metric on every single evaluation benchmark (such as surface normal prediction on NYUv2 or CelebA classification where FAMO slightly outperforms it). Additionally, the method requires per-task backward passes that scale computationally with task count, focuses solely on optimization-based approaches without custom architecture co-design, and did not evaluate augmented Nash-MTL on reinforcement learning benchmarks due to implementation unavailability.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): While IMGrad does not achieve the best performance, it consistently ranks among the top methods, underscoring the importance of imbalance sensitivity for learning massive tasks.
Generalizability Gap: The authors evaluated IMGrad exclusively on computer vision datasets (NYUv2, Cityscapes, CelebA) and simulated robotic manipulation benchmarks (Meta-World MT10); the authors did not evaluate the method on natural language processing, multilingual or code-switched text corpora, speech processing, large language model multi-task fine-tuning, or physical robotic hardware.
Methodological Gap: IMGrad requires computing individual task gradients for all tasks at each training step, incurring linear gradient computation overhead; furthermore, the method relies on a geometric proxy (cos theta between g_0 and g^m) to regulate imbalance sensitivity rather than directly resolving underlying curvature discrepancies across task loss surfaces.
Future Work: Extending imbalance-sensitive multi-task gradient descent methods to natural language processing, speech, and multimodal foundation models.; Developing scalable gradient combination algorithms to reduce the per-task gradient computation overhead in massive multi-task settings.; Exploring alternative geometric, statistical, or curvature-based formulations for quantifying task imbalance dynamically during training.; Investigating official implementations and extensions of augmented bargaining-game multi-task frameworks (such as Nash-MTL) in multi-task reinforcement learning environments.

Title: Leveraging Multi-Task Learning in Code-Switched setting
Authors: Mithun Kumar S R; Omkar Pitale; Aruna Malapati
Venue: Research Square
Domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Code-Switching / Code-Mixing (specifically Hindi-English / Hinglish token classification)
Problem Statement: Developing reliable natural language processing models for code-switched text is difficult due to the scarcity of annotated transcriptions and training data. This study investigates whether multi-task learning with shared representations between related token classification tasks (Language Identification and Named Entity Recognition) can leverage auxiliary training signals to improve model generalizability and task performance in code-switched environments.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-task learning using hard parameter sharing and homoscedastic uncertainty loss weighting for joint representation learning across related token classification tasks.
Methodology: The authors designed a stacked neural architecture consisting of a pre-trained multilingual transformer encoder (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa base, or XLM-RoBERTa large), a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network, and shared Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers. The shared representations feed into task-specific heads composed of MLP layers with GELU activations and Layer Normalization coupled with Conditional Random Field (CRF) sequence decoders. The framework is trained jointly for Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Language Identification (LID) using an adaptive multi-task loss function weighted by homoscedastic uncertainty.
Datasets and Benchmarks: LinCE (Linguistic Code-Switching Evaluation) benchmark for Hindi-English (Named Entity Recognition and Language Identification tasks)
Evaluation and Metrics: method: 10-fold cross-validation with early stopping, learning rate scheduling, and paired Student's t-test for statistical significance validation.; metrics: (NER average F1: {'mBERT': 71.37, 'XLM-RoBERTa_base': 77.41, 'XLM-RoBERTa_large': 82.92}, LID average F1: {'mBERT': 80.648, 'XLM-RoBERTa_base': 88.154, 'XLM-RoBERTa_large': 88.557}, paired t test p values: {'mBERT': 0.297, 'XLM-RoBERTa_base': 0.392, 'XLM-RoBERTa_large': 1.0})
Key Findings: Multi-task learning with hard parameter sharing outperforms single-task baselines by providing an implicit data augmentation effect that improves model generalizability in code-switched settings.; Joint training of Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Language Identification (LID) allows the NER task to benefit from representations learned during the LID task, yielding substantial performance gains.; XLM-RoBERTa large achieves the highest average F1 score for both NER (82.92%) and LID (88.557%), substantially outperforming mBERT (71.37% NER, 80.648% LID) and XLM-RoBERTa base (77.41% NER, 88.154% LID).; Adaptive loss weighting based on homoscedastic uncertainty prevents performance degradation across tasks compared to simple loss summation.; Paired Student's t-test analysis confirms that variations across cross-validation splits are not statistically divergent (p > 0.05).
Scope and Delimitations: The study restricts its empirical evaluation to two token classification tasks: Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Language Identification (LID).; The evaluation focuses exclusively on Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-switched text from the LinCE benchmark.; The model backbone comparisons are confined to mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa base, and XLM-RoBERTa large encoders stacked with BiLSTM and CRF layers.; Sentence lengths are fixed at a maximum of 64 tokens with a batch size of 32.
Limitations (Summary): The authors evaluated the framework exclusively on the LinCE Hindi-English dataset without conducting empirical validations on the broader GLUECoS benchmark or on other language pairs. Additionally, naive loss summation caused performance imbalances across tasks, necessitating uncertainty-weighted loss tuning.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): We are yet to experiment on GLUECoS dataset and try out more optimizations in order to achieve much better results than the existing ones.
Generalizability Gap: The proposed multi-task architecture has only been evaluated on Hindi-English code-switched text for NER and LID token classification. Its performance and generalizability across other code-switched language pairs (such as Spanish-English, Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian Arabic, or Nepali-English), other benchmarks like GLUECoS, and higher-level NLP tasks (such as sentiment analysis, question answering, and natural language inference) remain unverified.
Methodological Gap: The study limits its architectural design to hard parameter sharing with BiLSTM-CRF sequence classification heads, without examining soft parameter sharing mechanisms, cross-task attention, generative transformer architectures, or the empirical effects of pairing dissimilar tasks.
Future Work: Evaluate the multi-task framework on the GLUECoS benchmark dataset.; Implement and test additional optimization strategies to improve downstream task metrics.; Analyze specific task combinations to determine which task pairs optimize shared representations and improve generalizability.; Investigate the effects of implicit data augmentation from multi-task learning when training on similar versus dissimilar tasks.

Title: LibMTL: A Python Library for Deep Multi-Task Learning
Authors: Baijiong Lin; Yu Zhang
Venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR)
Domain: Deep Multi-Task Learning, Computer Vision, and Machine Learning Systems
Problem Statement: Most state-of-the-art multi-task learning models are implemented across fragmented codebases with divergent experimental protocols or lack public implementations entirely, which creates barriers to reproducible benchmarking, complicates the development of novel multi-task algorithms, and impedes the practical deployment of multi-task learning systems in real-world applications.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-task learning formalization with shared parameters theta and task-specific parameters psi for T tasks under single-input and multi-input settings, structured on an orthogonal decomposition between neural network architecture design and multi-objective loss or gradient balancing optimization strategies.
Methodology: LibMTL provides a modular, extensible PyTorch library structured into decoupled functional modules. The library includes LibMTL.config for command-line parameter handling, Dataloader for single-input and multi-input batch loading, LibMTL.model for backbone networks such as ResNet, LibMTL.architecture for 8 multi-task architectures (Hard Parameter Sharing, Cross-stitch Networks, MMoE, MTAN, CGC, PLE, Learning to Branch, and DSelect-k), LibMTL.loss for task loss definitions, LibMTL.weighting for 13 loss-balancing and gradient-balancing optimization strategies (Equal Weighting, GradNorm, Uncertainty Weights, MGDA, Dynamic Weight Average, Geometric Loss Strategy, PCGrad, GradDrop, IMTL, Gradient Vaccine, CAGrad, Nash-MTL, and Random Loss Weighting) supporting exact parameter gradients and representation gradient approximations, LibMTL.metrics for evaluation tracking, LibMTL.Trainer for unified execution, and LibMTL.utils for auxiliary training routines.
Datasets and Benchmarks: NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding benchmark containing 3 dense prediction tasks: 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pixel Accuracy (PAcc) for semantic segmentation; Absolute Error (AErr) and Relative Error (RErr) for depth estimation; Mean angle distance, Median angle distance (MED), and percentage of pixels within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° error thresholds for surface normal prediction]; baselines: [13 optimization strategies evaluated on the Hard Parameter Sharing architecture: Equal Weighting (EW), GradNorm, Uncertainty Weights (UW), MGDA, Dynamic Weight Average (DWA), Geometric Loss Strategy (GLS), Projecting Conflicting Gradient (PCGrad), GradDrop, Impartial Multi-Task Learning (IMTL), Gradient Vaccine (GradVac), Conflict-Averse Gradient descent (CAGrad), Nash-MTL, and Random Loss Weighting (RLW); 8 neural network architectures evaluated under the Equal Weighting strategy: Hard Parameter Sharing (HPS), Cross-stitch Networks, Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE), Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN), Customized Gate Control (CGC), Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE), Learning to Branch (LTB), and DSelect-k; Qualitative comparative analysis against existing multi-task learning toolkits including RMTL and MTLV]; architectures: [ResNet backbone feature extractor combined with multi-task parameter sharing heads and task-specific decoders for indoor scene understanding]
Key Findings: LibMTL provides a unified, extensible PyTorch library that supports 13 optimization strategies and 8 deep architectures, and allows flexible combinations across single-input and multi-input multi-task learning paradigms.; On the NYUv2 benchmark using the Hard Parameter Sharing architecture, the Geometric Loss Strategy achieves the highest semantic segmentation performance (54.59 mIoU, 76.06% PAcc) and lowest depth estimation errors (0.3785 AErr, 0.1555 RErr), while CAGrad achieves the lowest surface normal errors (22.47° Mean, 15.71° MED, 37.77% within 11.25°).; On the NYUv2 benchmark using the Equal Weighting strategy, MTAN achieves the highest semantic segmentation performance (54.64 mIoU, 75.99% PAcc) and lowest depth errors (0.3771 AErr, 0.1557 RErr), whereas Progressive Layered Extraction (PLE) and Customized Gate Control (CGC) achieve the lowest surface normal prediction errors (PLE reaches 22.10° Mean, 15.34° MED; CGC reaches 22.14° Mean, 15.33° MED).; The modular design cleanly decouples data loaders, loss functions, metrics, configurations, model backbones, parameter sharing architectures, and gradient weighting strategies, which allows researchers to implement new algorithms or apply existing methods to new applications with minimal code overhead.; Comparative analysis shows that LibMTL provides broader deep neural network support, more contemporary gradient-balancing algorithms, and greater task configuration flexibility than earlier specialized libraries such as RMTL and MTLV.
Scope and Delimitations: Implemented specifically for deep multi-task learning using the PyTorch framework.; Evaluated benchmark performance exclusively on the NYUv2 indoor scene understanding dataset across 3 dense prediction tasks (semantic segmentation, depth estimation, surface normal prediction) with a ResNet backbone.; Restricted empirical benchmark tables to testing individual optimization algorithms on Hard Parameter Sharing and testing individual architectures under Equal Weighting, rather than running full combinatorial matrices across all strategies and architectures.; Focused on supervised multi-task learning under single-input and multi-input formulations, excluding reinforcement learning and unsupervised multi-task setups.
Limitations (Summary): The authors acknowledge that exact gradient balancing methods demand substantial computation when models contain large numbers of shared parameters or tasks, which requires using representation gradient approximations. Furthermore, the library initially did not include transformer backbones or natural language tokenization models, and empirical benchmark evaluations were restricted to a single computer vision dataset.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Moreover, gradient balancing methods need to calculate the gradients of the task-shared parameters θ for every task, which may be computationally intensive when the number of shared parameters or tasks is large.
Generalizability Gap: The empirical benchmark in the paper is restricted to a single indoor RGB-D computer vision dataset (NYUv2); the authors did not evaluate the performance, memory footprint, and scaling properties of the library on large-scale natural language processing corpora, recommender systems, speech processing, tabular data, or multimodal foundation models.
Methodological Gap: The benchmark experiments evaluate optimization strategies only on the standard Hard Parameter Sharing architecture and evaluate architectures only under naive Equal Weighting, leaving the empirical interaction effects between advanced architectures (such as MTAN or PLE) and advanced gradient balancing methods (such as CAGrad or Nash-MTL) unexplored; additionally, exact gradient computation methods scale poorly in memory and time when the parameter count or task count increases without feature-level gradient approximations.
Future Work: Continuously maintaining and updating the library to incorporate newly proposed multi-task learning architectures and optimization strategies.; Updating the documentation and providing expanded user tutorials for complex multi-task workflows.; Adding multi-task learning application examples and benchmark suites from diverse domains beyond computer vision.; Providing additional neural network backbone models such as Vision Transformers and N-gram language representations.

Title: Lost in the Mix: Evaluating LLM Understanding of Code-Switched Text
Authors: Amr Mohamed; Yang Zhang; Michalis Vazirgiannis; Guokan Shang
Domain: Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, Code-Switching and Code-Mixing, Multilingual Language Understanding, Reading Comprehension, Multi-Domain Reasoning, Natural Language Inference
Problem Statement: How Large Language Models (LLMs) comprehend and reason over code-switched (mixed-language) text across different switching directions, language pairs, and linguistic constraints, and whether multilingual proficiency reflects genuine semantic comprehension or superficial pattern matching.
Theoretical Framework: Sociolinguistic and grammatical theories of code-switching, specifically the Equivalence Constraint Theory (Poplack, 1978) and the Matrix Language Frame model (Myers-Scotton, 1993), which govern permissible grammatical boundaries, matrix language frame preservation, and syntactic well-formedness in mixed-language discourse.
Methodology: A controlled multi-step LLM-centric generation pipeline using Claude 3.5 Sonnet to construct linguistically grounded noun-token code-switched variants (governed by Equivalence Constraint Theory and Matrix Language Frame rules) and random ratio-token (20%) variants of Belebele, MMLU, and XNLI across five typologically diverse languages (English, Arabic, German, French, Chinese); systematic zero-shot benchmarking across eight open-source LLMs (LLaMA 3.2 3B, LLaMA 3.1 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 3B/7B/72B, Mistral 7B v0.3, ALLaM 7B) using EleutherAI LM Evaluation Harness; switching-direction ablations reversing matrix and embedded languages; extreme multilingual mixing ablations blending two to four embedded languages; and mitigation studies comparing instructional in-context learning (ICL) prompts against instruction fine-tuning on 14.6k synthetic code-switched TED Talk samples using LLaMA 3.1 8B.
Datasets and Benchmarks: Belebele (parallel reading comprehension benchmark across English, Arabic, German, French, and Chinese); MMLU / MMMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding multi-choice reasoning benchmark); XNLI (Cross-lingual Natural Language Inference benchmark); TED Talks Parallel Corpus (Qi et al., 2018; filtered English sentences >70 words with parallel Arabic, Chinese, French, and German translations used for instruction tuning)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Accuracy (proportion of correctly answered questions per benchmark); Weighted Average Accuracy (size-weighted mean accuracy across Belebele, MMLU, and XNLI); Accuracy Delta (performance difference between code-switched variant and monolingual baseline); Human Preference and LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4o) pairwise preference ratings for generation quality]; evaluated models: [LLaMA 3.2 Instruct (3B); LLaMA 3.1 Instruct (8B, 70B); Qwen 2.5 Instruct (3B, 7B, 72B); Mistral 7B Instruct (v0.3); ALLaM 7B]; baseline comparisons: [Monolingual English Baseline (accuracy: 0.54 to 0.70 across models); Monolingual Non-English Baselines (Arabic, German, French, Chinese); Placeholder Baseline ('####' token substitutions isolating structural disruption from foreign semantics; accuracy: 0.41 to 0.59)]; key results: (noun token csw en matrix: Accuracy consistently drops across all models (LLaMA 3B: 0.47-0.50 vs 0.54; LLaMA 70B: 0.66-0.67 vs 0.70; Qwen 72B: 0.65-0.66 vs 0.69). All models outperform placeholder baselines., ratio token csw en matrix: Random 20% token substitutions cause comparable degradation to noun substitutions (LLaMA 3B: 0.43-0.51 vs 0.54; LLaMA 70B: 0.67-0.68 vs 0.70; Qwen 72B: 0.66 vs 0.69)., reverse csw non en matrix: Embedding English tokens into non-English matrix sentences consistently improves accuracy for lower-resource conditions (Mistral 7B Arabic: 0.35 to 0.48; Qwen 3B Arabic: 0.40 to 0.48; ALLaM 7B Chinese: 0.44 to 0.51)., extreme multilingual mixing: Mixing 2 to 4 languages in English matrix sentences reduces MMLU accuracy by 0.03 to 0.07 across models regardless of script type., icl mitigation: Yields inconsistent results (+0.01 to +0.07 for Qwen and ALLaM; -0.01 to -0.18 for LLaMA and Mistral)., model finetuning mitigation: Fine-tuning LLaMA 8B on 14.6k CSW generation samples produces consistent accuracy gains on comprehension benchmarks across all embedded languages while preserving monolingual English accuracy.)
Key Findings: Linguistically constrained code-switching systematically impairs comprehension: inserting foreign noun tokens into English sentences consistently degrades LLM accuracy across all evaluated model families, scales, and reasoning tasks, even when switches strictly adhere to Equivalence Constraint Theory and Matrix Language Frame rules.; Asymmetry in code-switching direction reveals an English-centric representational bias: while embedding non-English tokens into English matrix sentences reduces performance, embedding English tokens into non-English matrix sentences consistently improves comprehension (for example, Mistral 7B accuracy increases from 0.35 to 0.48 in Arabic), indicating that English acts as a facilitative anchor in multilingual pretraining representations.; Syntactic well-formedness provides limited mitigation: random ratio-token substitutions (20%) cause degradation comparable in magnitude to linguistically grounded noun-token substitutions, demonstrating that performance decline stems from representational interference in multilingual token integration rather than purely grammatical disruption.; Meaningful foreign tokens outperform semantic disruption: all models score substantially higher on code-switched inputs than on placeholder baselines ('####'), proving that LLMs partially recover and leverage semantic information from embedded foreign tokens.; In-context learning (ICL) mitigation yields inconsistent, architecture-dependent effects: meta-instruction cues improve performance for models with extensive multilingual pretraining (Qwen and ALLaM, gaining up to +0.07), but degrade performance for models with less cross-lingual alignment (LLaMA and Mistral, dropping up to -0.18).; Model-based instruction fine-tuning on synthetic CSW data provides robust, stable recovery: fine-tuning LLaMA 8B on 14.6k synthetic code-switched generation samples yields consistent accuracy gains across all embedded languages on downstream comprehension tasks without sacrificing monolingual English accuracy.
Scope and Delimitations: The study focuses on evaluating LLM comprehension and reasoning on multi-choice question answering and natural language inference rather than generative conversational dialogue or surface-level classification tasks.; Evaluations are delimited to five typologically diverse languages (English as primary matrix, alongside Arabic, German, French, and Chinese) representing varying scripts, families, and pretraining data representation levels.; Code-switching generation is primarily delimited to intra-sentential noun-token substitutions adhering to Equivalence Constraint Theory (ECT) and Matrix Language Frame (MLF) models, alongside a 20% random ratio-token substitution setup.; Evaluations are restricted to eight open-weight instruction-tuned decoder-only LLMs (LLaMA 3.2 3B, LLaMA 3.1 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 3B/7B/72B, Mistral 7B v0.3, ALLaM 7B).; Evaluation datasets rely on synthetic code-switched variants generated from parallel multilingual benchmark corpora (Belebele, MMLU, XNLI) rather than naturalistic spontaneous human conversational transcripts.
Limitations (Summary): The authors acknowledge that their evaluation relies on noun-token substitutions, which represents only a basic form of linguistically grounded switching, whereas more complex switching structures could cause greater degradation; the random ratio-token experiment is restricted to a single fixed substitution rate of 20% without testing rate variations; and the benchmarks are synthetically generated from parallel corpora, which, despite human verification, may not capture all nuances, informalities, and pragmatic dynamics of spontaneous human code-switching.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): While our study adopts a controlled evaluation setup for both linguistically and non-linguistically motivated code-switching, the noun-token approach we employ reflects one of the fundamental forms of linguistically grounded, naturalistic switching. However, more complex forms of codeswitching may induce more severe performance degradation. Future work should investigate how higher-complexity switching patterns affect LLMs' understanding. Additionally, in our non-linguistically motivated ratio-token experiments, the substitution rate was fixed at 20%. Exploring how variation in this ratio affects model behavior could yield a more nuanced understanding of the impact of non-linguistically grounded switching on LLM comprehension. Finally, our benchmarks are synthetically constructed yet human-verified to ensure linguistic naturalness, and this controlled design enables reproducible analysis of how LLMs process mixedlanguage inputs, even if it does not capture all nuances of spontaneous human code-switching.
Generalizability Gap: The findings are restricted to five high-to-mid resource languages (English, Arabic, German, French, and Chinese) and do not evaluate low-resource language pairs, dialects (such as regional Arabic or colloquial Tagalog-English/Hinglish), or trilingual and multi-party conversational settings. Additionally, the study evaluates only synthetic intra-sentential noun substitutions and 20% random token replacements, leaving open how models generalize to spontaneous conversational code-switching, clause-level switching, speech/multimodal inputs, or low-resource non-Latin scripts.
Methodological Gap: The study relies on synthetic LLM-generated code-switched benchmarks constructed from parallel corpora rather than authentic human-generated code-switched dialogues; it tests a fixed 20% substitution rate for random switching rather than exploring a continuous spectrum of switch densities; and it investigates fine-tuning mitigation on a single architecture and scale (LLaMA 3.1 8B) on a relatively small corpus (14.6k samples) without evaluating pretraining-stage code-switched objectives or larger multi-model fine-tuning suites.
Future Work: Investigating how higher-complexity switching patterns (such as phrase-level, clause-level, and inter-sentential code-switching) affect LLM comprehension.; Exploring variations in token substitution rates across a wider spectrum to systematically measure the dose-response relationship between switch density and model degradation.; Developing and evaluating pretraining paradigms and scalable instruction-tuning regimes that natively incorporate code-switching as a first-class linguistic phenomenon to mitigate English-centric representational bias.; Extending code-switching evaluation frameworks to spontaneous conversational human datasets, low-resource language pairs, and spoken or multimodal interaction settings.

Title: Multi-Task Deep Neural Networks for Natural Language Understanding
Authors: Xiaodong Liu; Pengcheng He; Weizhu Chen; Jianfeng Gao
Venue: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2019)
Domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Natural Language Understanding (NLU), Multi-Task Learning, Domain Adaptation, Pre-trained Language Models
Problem Statement: How to combine multi-task learning and unsupervised language model pre-training into a unified neural representation learning architecture that leverages cross-task supervision, provides regularization across tasks, and enables sample-efficient domain adaptation across diverse natural language understanding benchmarks.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-task learning principles (Caruana, 1997; Zhang & Yang, 2017) wherein joint representation learning across related tasks provides an inductive bias and regularization effect that alleviates overfitting to specific tasks, combined with bidirectional Transformer language model pre-training (BERT) using masked language modeling and next sentence prediction (Devlin et al., 2018; Vaswani et al., 2017), and multi-step reasoning via Stochastic Answer Networks (Liu et al., 2018a).
Methodology: MT-DNN extends BERT by incorporating multi-task learning across shared lower layers and specialized task-specific output layers. The shared layers consist of a lexicon encoder and a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder initialized with pre-trained BERT weights (BERT-Base or BERT-Large). The top layers implement specialized output heads for four distinct NLU task categories: (1) single-sentence classification using softmax logistic regression on the [CLS] embedding; (2) text similarity regression using linear projection on the [CLS] embedding optimized with mean squared error; (3) pairwise text classification using the Stochastic Answer Network (SAN) multi-step reasoning module with stochastic prediction dropout; and (4) relevance ranking (QNLI) formulated as pairwise learning-to-rank using cross-entropy loss over positive and negative candidate answers. The model undergoes a two-stage training process: unsupervised BERT pre-training followed by multi-task mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (SGD with Adamax optimizer) across all training tasks, and optional task-specific fine-tuning or domain adaptation.
Datasets and Benchmarks: GLUE Benchmark (General Language Understanding Evaluation): CoLA (8.5k train), SST-2 (67k train), MRPC (3.7k train), STS-B (7k train), QQP (364k train), MNLI (393k train), QNLI (108k train), RTE (2.5k train), WNLI (634 train); SNLI (Stanford Natural Language Inference, 549k train / 9.8k dev / 9.8k test); SciTail (Science Textual Entailment, 23.5k train / 1.3k dev / 2.1k test)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Matthews correlation coefficient (CoLA); Classification Accuracy (SST-2, RTE, WNLI, QNLI, SNLI, SciTail); Accuracy and F1 score (MRPC, QQP); Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients (STS-B); Matched and mismatched accuracy (MNLI-m/mm); GLUE benchmark macro average score]; baselines: [BiLSTM+ELMo+Attn (Wang et al., 2018); Single-task Pretrain Transformer / GPT (Radford et al., 2018); GPT on STILTs (Phang et al., 2018); BERT-Base and BERT-Large (Devlin et al., 2018); ST-DNN (Single-Task DNN ablation with SAN answer module and pairwise ranking loss without multi-task refinement); MT-DNN without fine-tuning (direct multi-task evaluation)]; benchmark results: (GLUE Test Score: {'MT-DNN': 82.7, 'BERT-Large': 80.5, 'Human_Performance': 87.1}, SNLI Test Accuracy: {'MT-DNN-Large': 91.6, 'BERT-Large': 91.0, 'GPT': 89.9}, SciTail Test Accuracy: {'MT-DNN-Large': 95.0, 'BERT-Large': 94.4, 'BERT-Base': 92.0}, Domain Adaptation SNLI 0.1% Data: {'MT-DNN': 82.1, 'BERT': 52.5}, Domain Adaptation SciTail 0.1% Data: {'MT-DNN': 81.9, 'BERT': 51.2})
Key Findings: MT-DNN achieves new state-of-the-art results on 10 NLU tasks across three major benchmarks (SNLI, SciTail, and 8 of 9 GLUE tasks), pushing the overall GLUE benchmark score to 82.7% (a 2.2% absolute improvement over BERT-Large).; Multi-task learning provides a strong regularization effect that mitigates task-specific overfitting and yields universal representations that transfer effectively across diverse downstream tasks.; Multi-task learning delivers the most substantial performance gains on tasks with small amounts of in-domain training data (such as RTE and MRPC compared to MNLI and QQP).; Representations learned by MT-DNN enable superior domain adaptation and sample efficiency, achieving 82.1% accuracy on SNLI and 81.9% accuracy on SciTail with only 0.1% of domain training samples, substantially outperforming BERT (52.5% and 51.2% respectively).; Formulating QNLI as a pairwise learning-to-rank task rather than binary classification significantly improves answer ranking accuracy.; Incorporating specialized task architectures like the Stochastic Answer Network (SAN) answer module into the representation framework improves pairwise text classification performance over standard linear classification heads.
Scope and Delimitations: Evaluated exclusively on English-language natural language understanding tasks spanning classification, similarity scoring, and ranking, excluding text generation, sequence labeling, multilingual tasks, and multimodal domains.; Restricted shared layer initializations to pre-trained BERT-Base and BERT-Large checkpoints with WordPiece tokenization and a maximum sequence length limit of 512 tokens.; Delimited domain adaptation experiments to textual entailment benchmarks (SNLI and SciTail) evaluated across discrete subsampling splits (0.1%, 1.0%, 10%, and 100%).; Employed hard parameter sharing across lower Transformer layers with task-specific output heads, without investigating soft parameter sharing or dynamic routing mechanisms.
Limitations (Summary): MT-DNN underfits unique tasks such as CoLA during multi-task training because isolated task definitions and small sample sizes prevent the model from benefiting from cross-task transfer without dedicated fine-tuning. In addition, MT-DNN does not explicitly model task relatedness or structured linguistic priors, does not surpass majority voting on the problematic WNLI dataset, and lacks verified defense against adversarial perturbations.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Our analysis shows that CoLA is a challenge task with much smaller in-domain data than other tasks, and its task definition and dataset are unique among all GLUE tasks, making it difficult to benefit from the knowledge learned from other tasks. As a result, MTL tends to underfit the CoLA dataset. In such a case, fine-tuning is necessary to boost the performance.
Generalizability Gap: The MT-DNN framework was evaluated exclusively on standard English NLU benchmarks (GLUE, SNLI, SciTail) with sequence lengths up to 512 tokens; the authors did not test generalization to non-English languages, cross-lingual transfer settings, low-resource dialects, long-document understanding, conversational dialogue systems, or generative sequence-to-sequence tasks.
Methodological Gap: MT-DNN employs uniform mini-batch sampling without dynamic task weighting or formal task covariance modeling to balance gradients and mitigate negative transfer; the hard parameter sharing framework treats all Transformer layers uniformly across tasks without adaptive routing; and the training procedure does not incorporate explicit syntactic or semantic linguistic structures or verify robustness against adversarial perturbations.
Future Work: Developing a deeper understanding of model structure sharing in multi-task learning.; Designing more effective training methods that leverage task relatedness among multiple tasks for both multi-task pre-training and fine-tuning.; Incorporating the linguistic structure of text into representation learning in a more explicit and controllable manner.; Verifying and improving the resilience and robustness of MT-DNN against adversarial attacks.
