Title: Multi-Task Disaster Tweet Classification Using Hybrid TF-IDF and Graph Convolutional Networks
Authors: Basudev Nath; Deepak Sahoo; Sudhansu Shekhar Patra; Hassan Alkhiri; Subrata Chowdhury; Sheraz Aslam; Kainat Mustafa
Domain: Crisis Informatics, Disaster Response, Social Media Natural Language Processing (Twitter/X Disaster Tweet Classification in English), Graph Neural Networks, Multi-Task Learning
Problem Statement: During crisis events, social media posts on X (formerly Twitter) provide critical situational information for emergency responders; however, the brevity, informality, high noise, and lexical sparsity of tweets impede automated classification. Existing machine learning methods produce high-dimensional sparse representations that struggle with noisy data, whereas deep learning and graph neural network approaches typically model either statistical term importance or relational dependencies in isolation rather than integrating both representations across multi-tiered disaster classification tasks.
Theoretical Framework: Graph-based text representation theory conceptualizing short-text classification via corpus-level word co-occurrence graphs with Normalized Pointwise Mutual Information (NPMI) edge weights and spectral Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), combined with statistical term weighting theory (TF-IDF) and cascaded multi-task representation learning through a shared Fully Connected Neural Network (FCNN).
Methodology: The authors developed a seven-stage cascaded multi-task learning framework combining statistical and graph-based representations. The pipeline pre-processes 33,370 tweets from CrisisNLP and CrisisLex using lowercasing, punctuation and stop-word removal, number replacement, entity anonymization, and Porter stemming. The architecture extracts fixed-length TF-IDF feature vectors (top k=20 terms) and builds a global word co-occurrence graph using a 5-word sliding window with NPMI edge weights filtered at a threshold of T=0.2. A dual-layer GCN (128 and 64 neurons with ReLU activations and cross-entropy loss) processes the graph to generate structural word embeddings. The framework concatenates the TF-IDF feature vectors and GCN embeddings into a fused representation Z = Z_TF-IDF ⊕ Z_GCN, which feeds into a shared two-layer FCNN (512 and 256 neurons with dropout, batch normalization, and L2 regularization) connected to sequential task-specific softmax classification heads: Task 1 for binary disaster identification (2 classes), Task 2 for multi-class disaster type categorization (3 classes: non-disaster, flood, earthquake), and Task 3 for aid and support need extraction in earthquake tweets (5 classes, balanced using SMOTE).
Datasets and Benchmarks: CrisisNLP and CrisisLex collected benchmark corpora containing 33,370 total disaster and non-disaster tweets; Task 1 Dataset: 33,370 total tweets partitioned into disaster (Target=1) and non-disaster (Target=0) classes, evaluated on 6,674 test samples under an 80:20 train-test split; Task 2 Dataset: 15,435 tweets pulled from Task 1 and structured into three balanced categories: earthquake (5,779 tweets), flood (4,873 tweets), and non-disaster (4,783 tweets), evaluated on 3,088 test samples; Task 3 Dataset: 5,779 earthquake-related tweets categorized into five support/aid classes (Donation & Volunteering, Food & Medicine, Infrastructure & Utilities, Other Useful Information, and Sympathy & Support), evaluated on 1,156 test samples with SMOTE oversampling applied during training
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Accuracy; Precision; Recall; Macro-averaged F1-score; Weighted-averaged F1-score; Confusion Matrix; Inference Latency and Throughput]; task 1 binary classification: (Proposed TF-IDF plus GCN: {'accuracy': '94.47%', 'precision': 0.9398, 'recall': 0.9491, 'f1_score': 0.9444}, TF-IDF Only: {'accuracy': '75.60%', 'precision': 0.7695, 'recall': 0.756, 'f1_score': 0.7567}, GCN Only: {'accuracy': '80.98%', 'precision': 0.8094, 'recall': 0.8098, 'f1_score': 0.8091}, Baselines: {'Bi-LSTM': '87.00% accuracy', 'LSTM-GAT': '88.40% accuracy', 'STGCN': '82.31% accuracy', 'HGAT': '80.45% accuracy', 'TextGCN': '80.31% accuracy'}); task 2 disaster type classification: (Proposed TF-IDF plus GCN: {'overall_accuracy': '91.78%', 'no_disaster_accuracy': '95.49%', 'flood_accuracy': '86.70%', 'earthquake_accuracy': '93.31%'}, GCN Only: {'overall_accuracy': '82.30%', 'no_disaster_accuracy': '84.50%', 'flood_accuracy': '80.40%', 'earthquake_accuracy': '82.10%'}, TF-IDF Only: {'overall_accuracy': '76.09%', 'no_disaster_accuracy': '77.73%', 'flood_accuracy': '74.08%', 'earthquake_accuracy': '76.74%'}); task 3 help category classification: (Proposed TF-IDF plus GCN: {'overall_accuracy': '94.64%', 'macro_average': {'precision': 0.921, 'recall': 0.9362, 'f1_score': 0.9278}, 'weighted_average': {'precision': 0.9446, 'recall': 0.9599, 'f1_score': 0.9518}, 'category_f1_scores': {'Donation_and_Volunteering': 0.9468, 'Food_and_Medicine': 0.9291, 'Infrastructure_and_Utilities': 0.8474, 'Other_Useful_Information': 0.9836, 'Sympathy_and_Support': 0.9425}}, Ablation and Baselines: {'TF-IDF_Only_accuracy': '54.01%', 'GCN_Only_accuracy': '62.89%', 'BERT_Infrastructure_f1': 0.22, 'LSTM_Infrastructure_f1': 0.22, 'Bi-LSTM_Infrastructure_f1': 0.37}); computational efficiency: (model parameters: approximately 2.3M parameters (compared to ~110M for BERT), inference speed: 217 tweets per second, average latency: 4.6 ms per tweet on NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU)
Key Findings: The hybrid TF-IDF + GCN framework outperformed standalone TF-IDF, standalone GCN, and deep learning baselines across all three evaluation tiers, achieving 94.47% accuracy on binary disaster identification, 91.78% on disaster type classification, and 94.64% on aid-need extraction.; Ablation experiments demonstrated that integrating local statistical term significance (TF-IDF) with global graph relational embeddings (GCN) produced large performance gains over single-representation models (+13.49% to +18.87% over TF-IDF alone; +9.48% to +31.75% over GCN alone across the three tasks).; On granular help-seeking categorization (Task 3), the hybrid model achieved strong macro-averaged F1 (0.9278) and significantly outperformed deep learning baselines (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, BERT), which struggled on minority aid categories such as Infrastructure & Utilities (BERT F1 = 0.22 vs. Hybrid F1 = 0.8474).; Detailed error analysis demonstrated that inter-disaster classification confusion was highly asymmetric in Task 2, where flood-related tweets were misclassified as earthquake events at six times the rate of the reverse error (107 instances vs. 18 instances), indicating shared crisis vocabulary between disaster types.; The proposed architecture achieved high computational efficiency with only 2.3 million parameters, processing 217 tweets per second with an average inference latency of 4.6 ms per tweet on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU.
Scope and Delimitations: The text corpus is delimited to English-language disaster tweets collected from the CrisisNLP and CrisisLex benchmark datasets.; The disaster typology is delimited to two natural hazard types (floods and earthquakes) alongside non-disaster content, excluding other disaster domains such as wildfires, cyclones, or human-induced crises.; The fine-grained help-seeking classification (Task 3) is delimited exclusively to earthquake-related tweets across five specific support categories.; The lexical feature extraction is constrained to the top k=20 TF-IDF terms per tweet based on empirical optimization, and the graph adjacency matrix is constrained by an NPMI edge threshold of T=0.2 using a 5-word sliding window.; The graph modeling relies on static corpus-level co-occurrence graphs rather than dynamic or streaming graph construction.
Limitations (Summary): The framework exhibits inter-disaster lexical confusion between flood and earthquake posts due to shared crisis terminology; the experimental evaluation is restricted to English-language static corpora across two natural disaster categories; Task 3 aid classification is evaluated only on earthquake tweets; and the system relies on static NPMI graphs without real-time streaming updates, geolocation features, or explainable AI mechanisms.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Large inter-disaster misunderstanding shows that flood and earthquake tweets share grammatical and contextual characteristics, while confusion with non-disaster content remains modest (43–74 instances). The misunderstanding is asymmetric, with Flood*rightarrow*Earthquake (107) being six times greater than Earthquake*rightarrow*Flood (18), suggesting that flood-related jargon is more commonly misinterpreted as earthquake terms.
Generalizability Gap: The framework was tested exclusively on English-language tweets covering two natural disaster types (floods and earthquakes) from historical CrisisNLP and CrisisLex datasets. The authors did not evaluate the approach on multilingual or code-mixed social media streams, non-English disaster communications, alternative disaster events (such as wildfires, typhoons, or industrial catastrophes), or multimodal posts containing paired images and text.
Methodological Gap: The framework depends on static corpus-level NPMI graph construction that cannot dynamically incorporate streaming real-time vocabulary or out-of-vocabulary disaster terms without retraining. Additionally, the methodology lacks geolocation-aware spatial analysis, comparison with large generative language models such as OpenAI GPT series, and post-hoc Explainable AI (XAI) mechanisms to provide transparent decision rationales for humanitarian responders.
Future Work: Extend the proposed hybrid framework to multilingual and code-mixed datasets to enhance linguistic diversity and geographic applicability.; Conduct comparative evaluations involving large-scale AI models, including OpenAI GPT-based classifiers, to assess scalability and adaptability.; Incorporate real-time data streaming and dynamic graph construction techniques to support live crisis monitoring.; Integrate geolocation-aware analysis to contextualize disaster reports and emergency support requests spatially.; Implement Explainable AI (XAI) methods to improve model transparency, interpretability, and operational utility in humanitarian decision-making.

Title: Multi-Task Learning as Multi-Objective Optimization
Authors: Ozan Sener; Vladlen Koltun
Venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2018)
Domain: Multi-Task Deep Learning and Multi-Objective Optimization (Computer Vision)
Problem Statement: Multi-task learning (MTL) is inherently a multi-objective optimization problem because tasks often compete and conflict for model capacity. Existing MTL methods commonly minimize a weighted linear combination of per-task losses, which requires expensive grid searches or heuristics and is only theoretically valid when tasks do not compete, failing to model task trade-offs and achieve Pareto optimality in high-dimensional deep networks.
Theoretical Framework: Gradient-based multi-objective optimization and Pareto optimality via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, leveraging the Multiple-Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA) and Frank-Wolfe optimization, along with an upper-bound formulation (MGDA-UB) proving that optimizing representations yields Pareto stationary solutions when the representation Jacobian is full-rank.
Methodology: The authors formulate multi-task learning as multi-objective optimization to find Pareto optimal solutions. They adapt the Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA) using a Frank-Wolfe optimizer with an exact analytical line search to solve the quadratic min-norm optimization in the convex hull of task gradients. To avoid scaling linearly with task count and gradient dimensions, they propose MGDA-UB (Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm – Upper Bound) for encoder-decoder architectures, which bounds the shared parameter objective by the norm of representation gradients using the chain rule. MGDA-UB optimizes representation gradients via a single backward pass over shared parameters, provably converging to a Pareto stationary point or a common descent direction assuming the Jacobian of the shared representation is full-rank.
Datasets and Benchmarks: MultiMNIST (MTL adaptation of MNIST with 60,000 overlaid digit image pairs for top-left and bottom-right classification tasks); CelebA (CelebFaces Attributes dataset with 200,000 face images annotated with 40 binary attribute classification tasks); Cityscapes (urban scene understanding dataset with pixel-level annotations for 19-class semantic segmentation, instance segmentation via center voting, and monocular depth estimation/disparity); ImageNet (used for pretraining the ResNet-50 shared encoder backbone for Cityscapes)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Classification accuracy (%) on top-left digit (task-L) and bottom-right digit (task-R) for MultiMNIST; Mean classification error (%) and attribute-wise binary classification error (%) across 40 facial attributes for CelebA; Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) for semantic segmentation on Cityscapes; Mean Squared Error (MSE) of normalized pixel-level center offset regression for instance segmentation on Cityscapes; Mean Squared Error (MSE) of disparity estimation for depth estimation on Cityscapes; Wall-clock training time (seconds/hours) and GPU computational acceleration factor]; baselines: [Uniform scaling (minimizing a uniformly weighted sum of loss functions); Single-task networks (solving each task independently with dedicated models); Grid search (exhaustive evaluation of static loss weight combinations); Uncertainty weighting (homoscedastic task uncertainty weighting by Kendall et al., 2018); GradNorm (gradient normalization algorithm by Chen et al., 2018); MGDA without approximation (full-parameter multiple gradient descent algorithm)]; architectures: [LeNet-based encoder with two task-specific fully-connected classification heads (MultiMNIST); ResNet-18 shared backbone (without final layer) with 40 task-specific 2048x2 linear heads (CelebA); Fully-convolutional ResNet-50 shared encoder with three task-specific Pyramid Pooling Module (PPM) decoders (Cityscapes)]
Key Findings: Formulating multi-task learning as multi-objective optimization with MGDA enables deep networks to find Pareto optimal solutions that effectively manage task trade-offs when tasks compete for model capacity.; On MultiMNIST, where competing tasks cause static scaling and heuristic weighting (Uncertainty Weighting, GradNorm) to underperform, MGDA-UB achieves digit classification accuracies comparable to dedicated single-task models (96.2% on task-L and 95.3% on task-R).; On the 40-task CelebA benchmark, MGDA-UB outperforms uniform scaling, single-task learning, uncertainty weighting, and GradNorm across the vast majority of attribute classification tasks, achieving the lowest average category error (8.95%).; On Cityscapes scene understanding, joint multi-task learning with MGDA-UB surpasses single-task and heuristic baselines across semantic segmentation (66.60 mIoU), instance segmentation (0.0104 MSE), and disparity estimation (0.0146 MSE).; MGDA-UB eliminates the computational bottleneck of standard MGDA by computing gradients with respect to shared representations via a single backward pass, accelerating training by 40% on Cityscapes (3 tasks) and by a factor of 25 on CelebA (40 tasks).; MGDA-UB achieves equal or slightly superior empirical accuracy compared to full-parameter MGDA because computing gradients in a lower-dimensional representation space reduces SGD gradient estimation variance and improves optimization stability.
Scope and Delimitations: Restricts theoretical guarantees and computational acceleration of MGDA-UB specifically to encoder-decoder and shared-trunk deep neural network architectures where task losses depend on a shared intermediate representation.; Assumes the Jacobian matrix of the shared representation with respect to shared parameters (dZ/d_theta_sh) is full rank to guarantee equivalence to Pareto stationarity.; Focuses on hard parameter sharing setups with gradient-based multi-objective optimization rather than soft parameter sharing or Bayesian prior regularization.; Evaluates on computer vision tasks (digit classification, facial attribute prediction, and dense scene understanding) with task counts ranging from 2 to 40.
Limitations (Summary): Standard gradient-based multi-objective optimization (MGDA) scales poorly with gradient dimensionality and scales linearly with the number of tasks due to requiring separate backward passes for each task. Although the MGDA-UB approximation mitigates this, it relies on an encoder-decoder structure and assumes the representation Jacobian matrix is full rank.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): However, there are two technical problems that hinder the applicability of MGDA on a large scale. (i) The underlying optimization problem does not scale gracefully to high-dimensional gradients, which arise naturally in deep networks. (ii) The algorithm requires explicit computation of gradients per task, which results in linear scaling of the number of backward passes and roughly multiplies the training time by the number of tasks.
Generalizability Gap: The proposed method was evaluated exclusively on computer vision benchmarks (MultiMNIST, CelebA, and Cityscapes); the authors did not evaluate the approach on natural language processing, speech recognition, reinforcement learning, cross-modal learning, or large-scale foundation models.
Methodological Gap: The MGDA-UB formulation is restricted to shared representation (encoder-decoder) architectures and requires the representation Jacobian to be non-singular (full rank); additionally, the method optimizes for arbitrary Pareto stationary points rather than allowing practitioners to target specific trade-off preferences along the Pareto front.
Future Work: Extending gradient-based multi-objective optimization and representation-level bounds to non-vision domains such as natural language processing, speech processing, and multi-agent reinforcement learning.; Developing multi-objective optimization algorithms for complex multi-task architectures beyond encoder-decoder structures, such as branched networks or soft parameter sharing.; Investigating methods to steer multi-objective optimization toward specific desired trade-off regions or target points along the Pareto front.

Title: Multi-Task Learning in Natural Language Processing: An Overview
Authors: Shijie Chen; Yu Zhang; Qiang Yang
Venue: Association for Computing Machinery
Domain: Natural Language Processing, Multi-Task Learning, Deep Learning, Pre-trained Language Models
Problem Statement: Deep neural models and pre-trained language models in natural language processing frequently encounter overfitting, data scarcity, and excessive computational adaptation costs when researchers train the models on isolated downstream tasks.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) principles wherein sharing inductive bias and complementary representations across related tasks improves model generalization and reduces sample complexity compared to isolated single-task learning.
Methodology: A comprehensive literature review and taxonomic categorization analyzing multi-task learning across four primary architectural paradigms (parallel, hierarchical, modular, and generative adversarial), multi-task optimization strategies (loss construction, gradient regularization, data sampling, and task scheduling), downstream application areas (auxiliary MTL and joint MTL), and benchmark datasets.
Key Findings: Multi-task learning architectures in natural language processing divide systematically into parallel architectures, hierarchical architectures, modular architectures, and generative adversarial architectures.; Modular multi-task learning mechanisms, including parameter-efficient adapters, prefix tuning, and hypernetworks, attain performance comparable to full model fine-tuning while reducing trainable parameter counts and storage requirements.; Optimization techniques such as uncertainty-based sampling, dynamic task scheduling, and gradient regularization prevent catastrophic forgetting and mitigate negative transfer across heterogeneous tasks.; Task relatedness substantially influences multi-task learning outcomes, where auxiliary tasks with high label entropy and balanced distributions provide greater performance gains than unrelated tasks.; Multi-task learning effectively alleviates data scarcity in low-resource languages and specialized domains by transferring shared representations from data-rich auxiliary tasks.
Scope and Delimitations: The authors focus specifically on the application of multi-task learning to downstream natural language processing tasks rather than general pre-training objectives.; The authors restrict the architectural taxonomy primarily to multi-task models containing task-specific trainable parameters, excluding general instruction tuning without task-specific parameters.; The authors examine deep learning approaches and exclude non-neural multi-task learning methods.
Limitations (Summary): The authors identify that determining optimal task combinations and establishing a formal understanding of task relatedness remain immature and unresolved challenges in multi-task learning.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Firstly, given multiple NLP tasks, how to find a set of tasks that could take advantage of MTL remains a challenge. Besides improving performance of MTL models, a deeper understanding of task relatedness could also help expanding the application of MTL to more tasks. Though there are some works studying this issue, as discussed in Section 4.4, they are far from mature.
Generalizability Gap: Existing research evaluates multi-task learning primarily on high-resource languages and standard benchmark tasks, leaving multi-task transfer in low-resource languages, multimodal environments, and interactive dialogue systems under-explored.
Methodological Gap: Current large pre-trained language models predominantly employ basic feature-sharing architectures during training, and existing task selection heuristics lack standardized quantitative metrics and theoretical guarantees across diverse task spaces.
Future Work: Developing theoretical and empirical frameworks to quantify task relatedness and systematically select beneficial task combinations.; Incorporating self-supervised and unsupervised learning techniques into multi-task learning to exploit unlabeled data and reduce dependence on human annotations.; Designing advanced multi-task architectures beyond simple feature sharing to improve pre-trained language models.; Extending multi-task learning to complex downstream applications, including dialogue systems and multimodal vision-language tasks.

Title: NTKMTL: Mitigating Task Imbalance in Multi-Task Learning from Neural Tangent Kernel Perspective
Authors: Xiaohan Qin; Xiaoxing Wang; Ning Liao; Junchi Yan
Venue: Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
Domain: Multi-task learning across multi-task computer vision dense prediction, molecular property regression, facial attribute classification, and multi-task reinforcement learning.
Problem Statement: Task imbalance in multi-task learning causes certain tasks to dominate shared parameter updates while other tasks suffer from insufficient optimization due to differing convergence speeds and loss dynamics.
Theoretical Framework: Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory and spectral analysis of gradient flow ordinary differential equations, which model convergence speeds of individual tasks through the eigenvalues of an extended multi-task NTK matrix.
Methodology: NTKMTL constructs an extended Neural Tangent Kernel matrix across tasks and normalizes task loss weights inversely proportional to the square root of the maximum eigenvalue of each task-specific NTK matrix scaled by the average maximum eigenvalue; NTKMTL-SR accelerates computation by calculating the NTK matrix over shared representations rather than full network parameters.
Datasets and Benchmarks: NYUv2; Cityscapes; CelebA; QM9; Meta-World MT10
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Mean Rank (MR); Average per-task performance drop relative to single-task learning baseline (Δm%); Semantic segmentation mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and pixel accuracy; Depth estimation absolute error and relative error; Surface normal mean error, median error, and percentage within angular thresholds (11.25°, 22.5°, 30°); Mean Absolute Error (MAE) across 11 quantum chemical regression properties; Multi-attribute classification accuracy across 40 facial attributes; Success rate across 10 robotic manipulation tasks]; baselines: [Single-task learning (STL); Linear Scalarization (LS); Scale-Invariant (SI); Dynamic Weight Average (DWA); Uncertainty Weighting (UW); Multi-Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA); Random Loss Weighting (RLW); PCGrad; GradDrop; CAGrad; IMTL-G; Nash-MTL; MoCo; Aligned-MTL; SDMGrad; DB-MTL; STCH; FAMO; FairGrad; GO4Align]
Key Findings: The convergence speed of each task in multi-task learning is governed by the eigenvalues of its task-specific Neural Tangent Kernel matrix, leading to spectral bias where tasks with larger eigenvalues dominate training.; Weighting tasks inversely proportional to the square root of their maximum NTK eigenvalue balances convergence speeds across tasks and mitigates task imbalance.; NTKMTL achieves state-of-the-art performance on the NYUv2 dense prediction benchmark with a mean rank of 4.33 and a relative performance drop of -6.99%, outperforming single-task learning across all three tasks.; On the CelebA 40-task benchmark, NTKMTL achieves an overall improvement over single-task learning (Δm% of -0.77%), outperforming all previous multi-task baselines.; NTKMTL-SR uses shared representations to achieve training speeds comparable to loss-oriented linear scalarization while attaining state-of-the-art results on the QM9 11-task regression benchmark (mean rank 4.00, Δm% 30.7%).; NTKMTL generalizes effectively to multi-task reinforcement learning on the Meta-World MT10 benchmark, achieving a 0.96 success rate.
Scope and Delimitations: Evaluated on supervised multi-task learning (2 to 40 tasks) and multi-task reinforcement learning (10 tasks).; Focuses optimization weight derivations primarily on the diagonal task-specific blocks of the extended NTK matrix.; NTKMTL uses mini-batch size n=1 for shared parameter calculations, while NTKMTL-SR uses mini-batch size n=4 on shared representations.
Limitations (Summary): The method relies solely on the diagonal task-specific blocks of the extended NTK matrix rather than modeling inter-task interactions present in the off-diagonal blocks, and NTKMTL-SR is difficult to apply in reinforcement learning settings where networks lack explicit separation between shared and task-specific heads.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): In this work, we proposed the extended NTK Ke for MTL as a tool for more comprehensive analysis of training dynamics across tasks. The weight design of our current method mainly focuses on the analysis of the task-specific NTK matrices Kii. The full structure of the extended NTK matrix Ke offers further analytical opportunities. For example, analyzing the off-diagonal Kij blocks could reveal novel insights into task interactions or guide the development of task grouping strategies. These potential avenues are left for future investigation.
Generalizability Gap: The method has not been evaluated on large-scale language models, multi-modal foundation models, or non-stationary online learning environments.
Methodological Gap: The weight calculation considers only the maximum eigenvalue of the task-specific NTK block rather than the complete eigenvalue spectrum or the off-diagonal task-interaction blocks of the extended NTK matrix.
Future Work: Analyzing the off-diagonal blocks Kij of the extended NTK matrix to model inter-task interactions.; Developing task grouping and task clustering strategies based on the full structure of the extended NTK matrix.; Extending shared representation approximations to policy architectures in multi-task reinforcement learning.

Title: Sentiment Analysis of Typhoon Related Tweets using Standard and Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks
Authors: Joseph Marvin R. Imperial; Jeyrome A. Orosco; Shiela Mae O. Mazo; Lany L. Maceda
Venue: arXiv
Domain: Crisis informatics, disaster response, and social media NLP (Twitter) in the Philippines during Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan), focusing on English and Filipino sentiment classification.
Problem Statement: Identifying and analyzing the underlying sentiments expressed in tweets posted by Filipino citizens before, during, and after Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) to understand social involvement, public empathy, and disaster-related communication patterns using standard and bidirectional recurrent neural networks.
Theoretical Framework: Supervised sequential modeling and sentiment analysis using recurrent neural architectures (standard RNN with truncated BPTT and bidirectional RNN with full BPTT) operating over continuous Word2Vec vector space word embeddings.
Methodology: A supervised sentiment classification pipeline comprising data collection via Twitter search for disaster hashtags (#YolandaPH, #BangonPH, #BangonPilipinas) between November 2013 and January 2014 (92,040 raw tweets), text preprocessing (deduplication, removal of usernames, URLs, retweets, emojis, stopwords, infrequent words, short words, and special characters leaving 39,867 tweets), continuous word representation using Word2Vec embeddings, balanced manual ground-truth annotation of 3,900 tweets across three classes (positive, negative, neutral; 1,300 per class), an 80/20 train/test split, hyperparameter tuning across batch sizes (64, 128), dropout rates (0.0, 0.5), and backpropagation through time configurations (truncated BPTT vs. full BPTT) for both standard and bidirectional RNNs on fine-grained and binary classification tasks, followed by corpus-wide inference on the remaining 35,967 unlabeled tweets.
Datasets and Benchmarks: 39,867 preprocessed Typhoon Yolanda tweets collected between November 1, 2013, and January 31, 2014, filtered from an initial corpus of 92,040 tweets gathered using the hashtags #YolandaPH, #BangonPH, and #BangonPilipinas; A manually annotated ground-truth benchmark of 3,900 balanced tweets (1,300 positive, 1,300 negative, and 1,300 neutral) split into an 80% training set (3,120 tweets) and a 20% test set (780 tweets); 35,967 unannotated disaster tweets classified during corpus-level sentiment distribution inference
Evaluation and Metrics: fine grained classification: (classes: ['positive', 'negative', 'neutral'], best model: Standard RNN, best hyperparameters: {'batch_size': 64, 'dropout': 0.5, 'bptt_type': 'truncated BPTT (tBPTT, value=50)', 'learning_rate': '1.80E'}, best accuracy: 0.8179, best f1 score: 0.8176, bidirectional rnn best accuracy: 0.8141, bidirectional rnn best f1 score: 0.8135); binary classification: (classes: ['positive', 'negative'], best model: Bidirectional RNN, best hyperparameters: {'batch_size': 64, 'dropout': 0.0, 'bptt_type': 'Full BPTT', 'learning_rate': '1.80E'}, best accuracy: 0.8769, best f1 score: 0.876, standard rnn best accuracy: 0.8712, standard rnn best f1 score: 0.8699); corpus inference distribution: (total inferred tweets: 35967, positive sentiment count: 18395, positive sentiment percentage: 0.511, neutral sentiment count: 10441, neutral sentiment percentage: 0.29, negative sentiment count: 7131, negative sentiment percentage: 0.198)
Key Findings: The standard RNN model configured with a batch size of 64, dropout rate of 0.5, and truncated BPTT achieved the highest accuracy of 81.79% and F1 score of 0.8176 for fine-grained 3-class sentiment classification.; The bidirectional RNN model configured with a batch size of 64, no dropout, and full BPTT achieved the highest accuracy of 87.69% and F1 score of 0.8760 for binary sentiment classification.; A batch size of 64 consistently outperformed a batch size of 128 across all tested model configurations, yielding accuracies above 80% across all evaluated runs.; Error analysis indicated that inaccuracies in both binary and fine-grained classification were predominantly caused by false negative misclassifications (accounting for 11.9% to 14% of errors).; Corpus-wide inference over 35,967 unannotated tweets using the best fine-grained model revealed that 51.1% of tweets were positive (prayers, hope, support, and gratitude), 29.0% were neutral (news reports, relief operation announcements, and citizen observations), and 19.8% were negative (sadness, despair, and grief for victims along with criticism of government relief mismanagement).
Scope and Delimitations: Restricted tweet collection to a specific historical time window between November 1, 2013, and January 31, 2014, corresponding to Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan).; Delimited data harvesting exclusively to three hashtags: #YolandaPH, #BangonPH, and #BangonPilipinas.; Delimited manual sentiment annotation to a balanced sample of 3,900 tweets (1,300 positive, 1,300 negative, 1,300 neutral) with an 80/20 train/test partition.; Constrained neural architectures to vanilla standard RNNs and bidirectional RNNs with Word2Vec word embeddings, excluding gated architectures (LSTM, GRU) and transformer models.; Delimited sentiment labels to three discrete categories (positive, negative, neutral) without fine-grained emotion sub-categorization (e.g., fear, gratitude, anger).
Limitations (Summary): The classification models exhibited persistent false negative misclassifications accounting for 11.9% to 14% of errors across binary and fine-grained tasks, and the study evaluated only basic standard and bidirectional RNN configurations without exploring multi-layer architectures or gated recurrent units.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): In the error analysis of binary classification, the cause of the 14% and 12% inaccuracy for standard and bidirectional models respectively is based on false negative misclassifications. Same case with the fine-grained classification, wherein 12% and 11.9% for standard and bidirectional models respectively were misclassified by the models as false negative. The error similarity is expected since the same dataset is used for both type of classifications. Moreover, it can be deduced that the complexity of finer-grained classification would result to slightly lower accuracy than binary classification since the datasets are being compared to three classes.
Generalizability Gap: The dataset and evaluation are restricted to a single catastrophic event (Typhoon Yolanda) in the Philippines during late 2013 and early 2014 using three specific hashtags; generalizability to other disaster categories (e.g., earthquakes, floods, volcanic eruptions), other typhoon events, diverse regional Philippine languages beyond English and Tagalog (e.g., Waray, Cebuano, Hiligaynon), and other social media platforms remains unproven.
Methodological Gap: The study utilized basic standard and bidirectional RNN models with Word2Vec embeddings rather than evaluating gated recurrent networks (LSTM, GRU), attention mechanisms, or pretrained contextual transformer architectures (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa). The evaluation was conducted on a single fixed 80/20 train/test split without k-fold cross-validation, out-of-domain robustness testing, or incorporation of multimodal and temporal social media metadata.
Future Work: Experimenting with different combinations and configurations of neural network layers in the hidden layer.; Exploring new architectures of Recurrent Neural Networks (such as LSTMs and GRUs) to improve classification performance on disaster-related text.

Title: The Decades Progress on Code-Switching Research in NLP: A Systematic Survey on Trends and Challenges
Authors: Genta Indra Winata; Alham Fikri Aji; Zheng-Xin Yong; Thamar Solorio
Venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2023
Domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Speech Processing, Code-Switching (CSW), Multilingual Language Modeling, Computational Linguistics
Problem Statement: A systematic investigation into decades of code-switching (CSW) research in natural language and speech processing to understand historical progress from linguistic theories to pre-trained neural language models, identify task and language coverage imbalances, evaluate dataset accessibility and attrition issues, and conceptualize open research challenges and future directions.
Theoretical Framework: Grammatical and linguistic constraint theories of bilingual code-switching, including Poplack's Equivalence Constraint (1980), Myers-Scotton's Matrix-Embedded Language Framework (MLF) (1997, 2005), and Belazi et al.'s Functional Head Constraint (1994), alongside cognitive theories of multilingual competence and cross-lingual representation alignment.
Methodology: Systematic literature survey and manual multi-annotator taxonomy coding analyzing over 400 papers published in the ACL Anthology (crawled up to October 2022) and ISCA proceedings using 14 code-switching search keywords. Three annotators categorized publications across language varieties (bilingual, trilingual, 4+; regional groups), publication venues, paper contribution genres, dataset sources/modalities, computational methodologies (rule-based/linguistic constraints, statistical methods, neural sequence models, pre-trained language models), and text/speech downstream tasks.
Key Findings: The vast majority of code-switching NLP research is bilingual with English as one of the pair (particularly South Asian languages like Hindi, Tamil, Malayalam, as well as Spanish and Chinese), while non-English pairs, Middle Eastern languages, and multilingual switching (trilingual or 4+) remain substantially under-represented.; Language identification and sentiment analysis dominate ACL text-based code-switching research, whereas ASR and TTS dominate ISCA speech processing publications, demonstrating ongoing fragmentation between the speech and text processing research communities.; Social media text and recorded conversational speech constitute the primary data sources, but over 60% of surveyed corpora are private/closed, and social media datasets suffer from significant data attrition due to URL-only sharing policies and deleted posts.; The methodological paradigm has shifted from rule-based linguistic constraints (Poplack's equivalence constraint, MLF, functional head constraint) and statistical models (CRF, SVM, HMM) to neural sequence architectures (RNN/LSTM) and pre-trained multilingual language models (mBERT, XLM-R).; While pre-trained multilingual language models enable end-to-end task performance without manual linguistic rules, they lack interpretability regarding failure modes and face catastrophic forgetting/language attrition when fine-tuned on mixed-language inputs.
Scope and Delimitations: The survey systematically indexes academic literature on code-switching published in open proceedings of the ACL Anthology (up to October 2022) and ISCA conferences, supplemented by curated public research repositories.; The scope covers both written natural language processing and spoken speech processing modalities across token-level, sequence-level, and generative tasks.; The analysis excludes papers published after October 2022 and excludes fine-grained categorization of code-switching types (such as intra-sentential versus inter-sentential switching) due to lack of reporting in source literature.; The survey is non-empirical and synthesizes findings and statistics across literature without running new experimental benchmarks or retraining models.
Limitations (Summary): The quantitative review is delimited to publications indexed in the ACL Anthology and ISCA proceedings (excluding broader journals and post-October 2022 literature), and does not categorize fine-grained linguistic switching types (such as intra-sentential vs. inter-sentential switching) because many surveyed papers omit these structural details.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): The numbers in this survey are limited to papers published in the ACL Anthology and ISCA Proceedings. However, we also included papers as related work from other resources if they are publicly available and accessible. In addition, the category in the survey does not include the code-switching type (i.e., intra-sentential, inter-sentential, etc.) since some papers do not provide such information.
Generalizability Gap: Code-switching research and resources are heavily skewed toward a few high-resource bilingual pairs involving English (Hindi-English, Spanish-English, Chinese-English). Geographic varieties, regional dialects, underrepresented indigenous languages, non-English mixed pairs, and complex multilingual interactions (trilingual and 4+ languages) remain severely understudied and lack generalizable models.
Methodological Gap: Pre-trained multilingual models lack interpretability in code-switched contexts, suffer from catastrophic forgetting and cross-lingual representation degradation, and remain under-evaluated for scaling laws and compute-performance trade-offs. Furthermore, evaluation methods for generative code-switched text rely heavily on subjective human evaluation, lacking automated metrics that reliably align with human judgments of fidelity, style mimicry, and discourse naturalness.
Future Work: Broadening language scope to under-represented code-switching styles, regional dialects, and non-English/multilingual (>2 languages) language combinations.; Developing open, accessible, and ecologically valid written code-switched corpora that avoid data attrition issues associated with social media APIs.; Investigating model scaling laws, compute-performance trade-offs, and zero-shot/few-shot prompt and instruction tuning with large multilingual foundation models on code-switched tasks.; Integrating code-switching evaluation into standardized cross-lingual benchmarks (e.g., XTREME-R, XGLUE) to assess model robustness and continual learning against catastrophic forgetting.; Creating complex reasoning and comprehension benchmarks for code-switched text, including natural language inference, coreference resolution, and question answering.; Developing code-switching conversational dialogue agents and generative models with automated evaluation metrics aligned with human judgments of quality, style, and naturalness.

Title: The Script Tax: Measuring Tokenization-Driven Efficiency and Latency Disparities in Multilingual Language Models
Authors: Aradhya Dixit; Shreem Dixit
Venue: arXiv
Domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Multilingual Language Models, Tokenization Efficiency and Fairness, Subword Fragmentation, Inference Latency
Problem Statement: Pretrained multilingual language models are often assumed to be script-agnostic, yet subword tokenizers can impose systematic computational, latency, and information-cost disparities on specific writing systems. When a tokenizer segments one orthography into substantially more subword fragments than another orthography representing identical linguistic content, the resulting sequence inflation increases memory consumption and inference latency while degrading modeling efficiency. Furthermore, standard token-level negative log-likelihood metrics fail to detect this inefficiency because predicting small subword units artificially lowers per-token loss.
Theoretical Framework: The conceptual framework of the script tax operationalizes tokenization disparities along three interrelated dimensions: tokenization fragmentation (measured by word fertility), inference computational overhead (governed by superlinear Transformer attention scaling relative to sequence length), and character-normalized information cost (measured via Bits Per Character to resolve the subword fragmentation negative log-likelihood paradox).
Methodology: The authors established a controlled paired evaluation framework comparing matched sentence pairs with identical linguistic content across two orthographic variants (Orthography A and Orthography B) using two multilingual masked language models (mBERT and XLM-R). The methodology quantifies the script tax across three primary axes: (1) tokenization fragmentation measured through token fertility (tokens per word) and fertility differences; (2) information efficiency measured through Bits Per Character (BPC), which normalizes masked-token loss by Unicode character count rather than subword token count; and (3) computational overhead measured through median inference latency and throughput on identical hardware. Additionally, the authors implemented a round-trip Character Error Rate (CER) check using bidirectional orthographic mapping functions to verify that measured performance differences originate from tokenizer mechanics rather than transliteration noise.
Datasets and Benchmarks: Paired parallel sentence corpus consisting of matched sentence pairs (D = {(x_A^(n), x_B^(n))}_{n=1}^N) expressing identical linguistic content across two orthographic variants (higher-fragmentation Orthography B versus lower-fragmentation Orthography A)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Fertility (tokens per word, tokens/word); Inference throughput (sentences per second); Median inference latency tax ratio (rho_lat); Bits Per Character (BPC, character-normalized loss in bits); Relative BPC increase percentage (delta_BPC); Round-trip Character Error Rate (CER_rt)]; evaluated models: [mBERT (Multilingual BERT); XLM-R (XLM-RoBERTa)]; quantitative results: (fertility: {'lower_fragmentation_orthography': '2.10 to 2.35 tokens/word', 'higher_fragmentation_orthography': '6.73 to 6.85 tokens/word', 'fertility_gap': '+4.38 to +4.75 tokens/word (~3.4x sequence expansion)'}, inference latency and throughput: {'lower_fragmentation_throughput': '~3.8 sentences/second', 'higher_fragmentation_throughput': '~0.23 sentences/second', 'slowdown_factor': '16.5x slowdown'}, information cost bpc: {'mBERT_bpc': '8.06 -> 9.65 bits/char (+19.7% increase)', 'XLM-R_bpc': '12.19 -> 17.94 bits/char (+47.1% increase)'}, robustness check: {'round_trip_cer': '0.31'})
Key Findings: Pretrained multilingual language models exhibit substantial tokenization fragmentation disparities across orthographic variants with identical linguistic content, resulting in a ~3.4x fertility increase (6.73 to 6.85 tokens/word versus 2.10 to 2.35 tokens/word).; Subword sequence inflation induces a 16.5x inference slowdown on identical hardware, reducing throughput from ~3.8 sentences/second to ~0.23 sentences/second due to superlinear attention scaling.; Character-normalized information cost (BPC) degrades substantially for the higher-fragmentation orthography (+19.7% for mBERT and +47.1% for XLM-R), demonstrating that token-level loss metrics conceal genuine representational inefficiency.; Round-trip Character Error Rate evaluation (CER_rt = 0.31) demonstrates that the observed performance gaps reflect tokenizer-induced processing behavior rather than dataset conversion noise.; Pretrained subword tokenizers create structural inequities in computational accessibility and representation quality across writing systems, demonstrating that tokenization choices directly govern multilingual model fairness.
Scope and Delimitations: Model scope is delimited to two multilingual masked language models: mBERT and XLM-R.; Linguistic evaluation is delimited to two orthographic variants expressing identical content within a paired sentence setup.; Experimental hardware evaluation is delimited to a single fixed hardware and inference configuration.; Evaluation scope is delimited to tokenization fertility, character-normalized masked language modeling loss (BPC), and inference latency, excluding downstream fine-tuning tasks and autoregressive generation.
Limitations (Summary): The authors identify three primary limitations: the study examines only two orthographic variants and two masked language models (mBERT and XLM-R), which may not capture the magnitude of disparities in other scripts or model families; the paired experimental design depends on an automated orthography conversion pipeline where residual conversion artifacts could affect results despite round-trip validation; and exact latency measurements depend on a specific hardware configuration, although relative performance penalties generalize qualitatively.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Our analysis is limited to two orthographic variants and two multilingual masked language models (mBERT and XLM-R), so the magnitude of the script tax may differ for other scripts, tokenizers, and model families. The paired setup relies on an orthography conversion pipeline; while round-trip CER (CERrt) offers a robustness check, residual conversion artifacts may still influence results. Finally, latency numbers depend on a specific hardware/inference configuration, though the relative penalties from sequence inflation should generalize qualitatively.
Generalizability Gap: The study evaluates only two orthographic variants and two encoder-only masked language models (mBERT and XLM-R), leaving unexamined autoregressive decoder-only architectures (modern generative LLMs), broader non-Latin scripts, and alternative hardware acceleration environments.
Methodological Gap: The evaluation relies on an orthographic conversion pipeline that exhibits imperfect round-trip reconstruction (CER_rt = 0.31), omits downstream task benchmarks (such as classification, question answering, or machine translation), and does not directly measure memory bandwidth or energy consumption during inference.
Future Work: Extending script tax measurements to broader writing systems, diverse tokenizer architectures, and autoregressive large language model families.; Designing script-aware tokenization interventions, including vocabulary augmentation, dynamic re-tokenization, and script-balanced pretraining.; Incorporating character-normalized loss metrics (BPC) and compute-aware latency metrics into standard multilingual NLP benchmark evaluations.; Refining bidirectional orthographic conversion pipelines to eliminate residual conversion noise in paired cross-script analyses.

Title: Tokenization Impacts Multilingual Language Modeling: Assessing Vocabulary Allocation and Overlap Across Languages
Authors: Tomasz Limisiewicz; Jiří Balhar; David Mareček
Venue: ACL 2023
Domain: Multilingual natural language processing, subword tokenization, and cross-lingual representation learning across diverse language families and writing systems.
Problem Statement: Investigating the influence of subword tokenization properties—specifically vocabulary allocation (representing language-specific lexical units) and vocabulary overlap (sharing lexical units across languages)—on multilingual language model representations and downstream task performance.
Theoretical Framework: Multilingual Transformer language models allocate a large proportion of parameters in the input embedding layer. The lexical representations learned by subword tokenizers determine the trade-off between cross-lingual parameter sharing (vocabulary overlap) and language-specific capacity (vocabulary allocation), which can be evaluated by probing frozen contextual representations.
Methodology: The authors introduced non-parametric metrics to evaluate tokenizers: Vocabulary Allocation measured via Average Rank (AR) and Characters Per Token (CPT), and Vocabulary Overlap measured via Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD). They compared SentencePiece Unigram LM, BPE, and two novel merging methods (NOOVERLAP and TOKMIX). They pre-trained scaled-down XLM-RoBERTa models (150M parameters) on balanced Common Crawl subsets (6 and 20 languages) and evaluated representations using masked language modeling (MRR) and frozen linear probing across word-level and sentence-level downstream tasks.
Datasets and Benchmarks: CC-100 (Common Crawl 10% balanced subsample for pre-training across 6 and 20 languages); Universal Dependencies (UD) for Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging and Dependency Tree Labeling; WikiANN for Named Entity Recognition (NER); XNLI (Cross-lingual Natural Language Inference); Tatoeba bitext corpus for cross-lingual sentence retrieval
Evaluation and Metrics: tokenizer metrics: [Average Rank (AR); Characters Per Token (CPT); Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD)]; model metrics: [Masked Language Modeling Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR); Macro-averaged F1 score for word-level tasks (POS tagging, NER, Dependency edge labeling); Classification accuracy for sentence-level NLI (XNLI); Cosine similarity alignment accuracy for sentence retrieval (Tatoeba)]; statistical analysis: Spearman rank correlation coefficients (with p-values) computed across multiple random seeds.
Key Findings: High vocabulary allocation (higher average rank and longer characters per token) significantly improves in-language results and cross-lingual transfer for word-level downstream tasks including POS tagging, NER, and dependency labeling.; Vocabulary overlap across languages benefits cross-lingual transfer for sentence-level semantic tasks (XNLI, Tatoeba sentence retrieval) and NER within the same script, but impairs performance on syntactic tasks (POS tagging and dependency labeling).; Completely eliminating vocabulary overlap (NOOVERLAP) achieves superior performance on POS tagging and dependency labeling among same-script languages, showing that shared surface strings with distinct cross-lingual meanings introduce negative interference for syntactic tasks.; Higher masked language modeling performance (MRR) negatively correlates with word-level downstream task performance because higher vocabulary allocation increases the candidate prediction space during masked pre-training while providing richer lexical features for downstream tasks.; Standard SentencePiece Unigram LM underperforms BPE and TOKMIX in multilingual vocabulary allocation, as its character n-gram initialization restricts vocabulary coverage for larger vocabulary sizes across most languages except Chinese.
Scope and Delimitations: Investigated a primary set of 6 typologically diverse languages (Arabic, Chinese, Greek, Turkish, Spanish, English) and extended to a broader set of 20 languages.; Pre-trained scaled-down XLM-RoBERTa architectures (8 layers, 6 attention heads, hidden dimension 768, 150M parameters) with a fixed vocabulary size of 120,000.; Evaluated representations via linear probes on frozen contextualized embeddings rather than full fine-tuning.; Pre-training was conducted on a 10% balanced sample of CC-100 data with an exponential smoothing parameter alpha = 0.25.
Limitations (Summary): The authors used scaled-down language models with 150M parameters to manage computational costs across multiple pre-training iterations, and evaluated the models using frozen linear probes rather than full end-to-end fine-tuning.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): To achieve robust, unbiased results, we decided to train first on a smaller number of languages, fix our methodology and then confirm our findings on the full set of languages. This meant that two rounds of pretraining needed to be done and because of that, we scaled our models down for computational efficiency reasons. Another limitation of our methodology is the choice to train linear probes on top of the contextualized word representations instead of the more common finetuning approach. Nevertheless, we think that probing gives better insight into the pretrained model's representation.
Generalizability Gap: The empirical findings are based on scaled-down 150M parameter models evaluated on up to 20 languages, which leaves uncertain whether the observed trade-offs between vocabulary allocation and overlap persist identically in large-scale foundation models (such as models with >300M to hundreds of billions of parameters) or across extremely low-resource languages.
Methodological Gap: The evaluation methodology relies exclusively on linear probing of frozen embeddings rather than full task-specific fine-tuning or parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), and the NOOVERLAP method could not be scaled to 20 languages due to per-language vocabulary partition constraints.
Future Work: Identifying optimal multilingual tokenization and vocabulary construction strategies to balance language-specific representation and cross-lingual sharing.; Evaluating vocabulary allocation and overlap dynamics in larger-scale multilingual language models.; Investigating tokenization behavior and vocabulary allocation on broader collections of low-resource languages and scripts.; Comparing linear probing insights with full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient adaptation methods.

Title: Transformer-based Multi-task Learning for Disaster Tweet Categorisation
Authors: Congcong Wang; Paul Nulty; David Lillis
Venue: Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Information Systems for Crisis Response and Management (ISCRAM 2021)
Domain: Crisis Informatics, Disaster Response, Social Media Natural Language Processing (Twitter/X Disaster Tweet Classification and Prioritization), Multi-Task Learning
Problem Statement: Manual identification of actionable disaster messages during crises is unfeasible due to explosive message volumes on social media. Emergency response operators require real-time categorization of crisis-related tweets by requested information types and accurate message prioritization to establish situational awareness, but single-task models and traditional classifiers struggle with cross-task dependencies, severe class imbalance, and diverse disaster contexts.
Theoretical Framework: Multi-task learning parameter-sharing theory (Zhang and Yang, 2017) positing that joint optimization across related downstream tasks regularizes representation learning, mitigates overfitting, and transfers inductive knowledge through a shared transformer encoder backbone; Situational Awareness (SA) framework in crisis response (Endsley, 2017; Vieweg et al., 2010).
Methodology: Proposed a transformer-based multi-task learning (MTL) framework combining multi-label Information Type Categorisation (ITC) across 25 categories and continuous Priority Estimation (PE) into a unified architecture. The framework shares an upstream transformer encoder (evaluating BERT_base, DistilBERT_base, ELECTRA_base, and ALBERT_base_v2) and adds two task-specific projection heads: a linear multi-label projection layer with sigmoid activation for ITC, and a linear regression projection layer for PE mapping categorical priority levels (Critical: 1.0, High: 0.75, Medium: 0.5, Low: 0.25) to continuous scores in [0, 1]. The joint model optimizes a composite loss combining binary cross-entropy for ITC and Mean Squared Error for PE with equal loss weighting (alpha = 0.5). To enhance generalization across heterogeneous encoders, introduced an ensemble technique combining disparate MTL models using a Union strategy for information type predictions and a Highest strategy for priority level predictions.
Datasets and Benchmarks: TREC Incident Streams (TREC-IS) benchmark dataset (40,459 total disaster tweets across 42 crisis events from 2018 to 2020A; partitioned into a training set of 30,420 tweets from the 2018, 2019A, and 2019B editions, a development set of 3,381 tweets [10% sample] for hyperparameter selection, and a held-out test set of 6,658 tweets across 15 crisis events from the 2020A edition; annotated with an ontology of 25 information types [6 actionable, 19 non-actionable] and 4 priority levels [critical, high, medium, low])
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [Ranking: Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG@100); Alerting Worth: Alert Worth High/Critical (AW-HC) and Alert Worth All (AW-A); Information Feed Categorisation: Actionable F1 (CF1-H), All F1 (CF1-A), Categorisation Accuracy (Cacc); Prioritisation: Priority Macro-F1 Actionable (PErr-H), Priority Macro-F1 All (PErr-A); Overall: Harmonic Mean (HarM) across normalized metrics]; baseline comparison: (Logistic Regression (LR + STL): {'NDCG': 0.4495, 'AW-HC': -0.4856, 'AW-A': -0.2627, 'PErr-H': 0.1718, 'PErr-A': 0.2216, 'CF1-H': 0.0898, 'CF1-A': 0.1527, 'Cacc': 0.9113, 'HarM': 0.2109}, BERT base (STL): {'NDCG': 0.4393, 'AW-HC': -0.4057, 'AW-A': -0.2148, 'PErr-H': 0.2402, 'PErr-A': 0.2758, 'CF1-H': 0.1084, 'CF1-A': 0.1801, 'Cacc': 0.896, 'HarM': 0.251}, BERT base + MTL (Proposed Individual): {'NDCG': 0.5101, 'AW-HC': -0.2689, 'AW-A': -0.1569, 'PErr-H': 0.1923, 'PErr-A': 0.2544, 'CF1-H': 0.1382, 'CF1-A': 0.1638, 'Cacc': 0.8937, 'HarM': 0.2609}); encoder ablation mtl: (BERT base (110M): {'NDCG': 0.5101, 'AW-HC': -0.2689, 'AW-A': -0.1569, 'PErr-H': 0.1923, 'PErr-A': 0.2544, 'CF1-H': 0.1382, 'CF1-A': 0.1638, 'Cacc': 0.8937, 'HarM': 0.2609}, DistilBERT base (66M): {'NDCG': 0.4808, 'AW-HC': -0.4533, 'AW-A': -0.2382, 'PErr-H': 0.9004, 'PErr-A': 0.1191, 'CF1-H': 0.1376, 'CF1-A': 0.183, 'Cacc': 0.211, 'HarM': 0.2264}, ELECTRA base (110M): {'NDCG': 0.5042, 'AW-HC': -0.4011, 'AW-A': -0.2122, 'PErr-H': 0.2059, 'PErr-A': 0.2801, 'CF1-H': 0.1514, 'CF1-A': 0.1742, 'Cacc': 0.8958, 'HarM': 0.2689}, ALBERT base v2 (11M): {'NDCG': 0.4669, 'AW-HC': -0.4118, 'AW-A': -0.219, 'PErr-H': 0.19, 'PErr-A': 0.272, 'CF1-H': 0.0568, 'CF1-A': 0.1707, 'Cacc': 0.9087, 'HarM': 0.1923}); ensemble results: (EnsembleA (BERT + ELECTRA): {'NDCG': 0.5207, 'AW-HC': -0.2274, 'AW-A': -0.1406, 'PErr-H': 0.1999, 'PErr-A': 0.256, 'CF1-H': 0.1738, 'CF1-A': 0.1796, 'Cacc': 0.8722, 'HarM': 0.2836}, EnsembleB (DistilBERT + ALBERT): {'NDCG': 0.4848, 'AW-HC': -0.3212, 'AW-A': -0.1823, 'PErr-H': 0.2081, 'PErr-A': 0.2728, 'CF1-H': 0.1407, 'CF1-A': 0.2041, 'Cacc': 0.8844, 'HarM': 0.2752}, EnsembleC (BERT + DistilBERT + ELECTRA): {'NDCG': 0.5206, 'AW-HC': -0.1982, 'AW-A': -0.1282, 'PErr-H': 0.2023, 'PErr-A': 0.2589, 'CF1-H': 0.1819, 'CF1-A': 0.1909, 'Cacc': 0.8621, 'HarM': 0.2919}, EnsembleD (BERT + DistilBERT + ELECTRA + ALBERT / Proposed Best): {'NDCG': 0.5176, 'AW-HC': -0.1613, 'AW-A': -0.1148, 'PErr-H': 0.2594, 'PErr-A': 0.2966, 'CF1-H': 0.1754, 'CF1-A': 0.2084, 'Cacc': 0.8545, 'HarM': 0.3141})
Key Findings: Multi-task learning with a shared BERT encoder backbone outperforms single-task learning baselines (both BERT STL and Logistic Regression STL), yielding superior ranking (NDCG 0.5101 vs. 0.4393) and alerting worth (AW-HC -0.2689 vs. -0.4057) while eliminating the operational requirement of training separate models for separate tasks.; Parameter-efficient transformer variants (DistilBERT at 66M parameters and ALBERT at 11M parameters) achieve competitive disaster tweet classification performance relative to full-sized encoders (BERT and ELECTRA at 110M parameters), demonstrating operational viability on resource-constrained hardware.; Combining diverse multi-task transformer models into an ensemble yields substantial performance gains, elevating the overall harmonic mean score (HarM) from 0.2609 (single BERT MTL) to 0.3141 (EnsembleD) and achieving state-of-the-art results across benchmark metrics.; Ensemble fusion ablations demonstrate that combining predictions via a Union strategy for information types and a Highest strategy for priority levels produces optimal performance across ranking, alerting worth, and categorization metrics.; The proposed multi-task framework and ensemble method achieved state-of-the-art performance when evaluated against participating systems in the TREC Incident Streams (TREC-IS 2020A) benchmark track across both 25-class (Task 1) and 12-class (Task 2) evaluations.; Qualitative error analysis indicates that misclassifications often arise from missing ground truth annotations, ambiguous multi-perspective interpretations (first-party versus third-party reporting), complex geographic entity disambiguation, and human assessor subjectivity.
Scope and Delimitations: The experimental evaluation is delimited to English-language disaster tweets from the TREC-IS 2018–2020A benchmark dataset covering 42 crisis events.; Input representations are delimited strictly to raw text sequences with a maximum length of 128 WordPiece tokens, excluding linked web articles, images, and author metadata.; Architectural exploration is delimited to four pre-trained uncased base-scale transformer encoders (BERT_base, DistilBERT_base, ELECTRA_base, ALBERT_base_v2) using hard parameter sharing across two downstream heads.; Multi-task optimization is delimited to an equal fixed loss weighting parameter (alpha = 0.5) combining binary cross-entropy and mean squared error.; Ensemble aggregation is delimited to heuristic rule-based fusion strategies (Union/Intersection and Highest/Average/Lowest) rather than learned stacking classifiers.
Limitations (Summary): The proposed approach is limited to processing raw textual tweet content without incorporating linked external web pages or multimodal imagery; the multi-task formulation is restricted to two downstream tasks evaluated on a single benchmark corpus; computational efficiency and real-time processing throughput during high-volume crisis surges have not been empirically evaluated; and evaluation relies on human assessor annotations that contain subjective inconsistencies and errors.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): Regarding the eectiveness, there is still much room to improve. We oer our approach as a baseline for future work on this problem. Our approach is currently limited to using the raw text of tweets. Per McCreadie et al. [2020,](#page-0-17) linked content such as the web pages, or images posted along with the tweets are likely to improve performance. Hence, future work will incorporate this linked information into our current approach. In addition, since our current approach only focuses on two tasks from a single corpus, we plan to extend our approach to support more tasks from multiple corpora. Although eectiveness is an essential performance measurement for an emergency response system, another aspect to which the same importance should be given is eciency. When employing an emergency response system in a real-world situation, the speed of message handling is crucial because social media message quantities are usually enormous during a crisis. Our approach has not yet been examined regarding its eciency, which also requires further exploration.
Generalizability Gap: The empirical evaluation is restricted to English-language Twitter posts across 42 disaster events in the TREC-IS benchmark, leaving unexamined performance on non-English crisis communications, code-switched microblogging streams, alternative messaging platforms (such as Facebook, Reddit, or Telegram), and multimodal disaster data streams containing synchronized imagery and geolocation coordinates.
Methodological Gap: The multi-task training setup uses a static, uniform loss weight parameter (alpha = 0.5) without exploring dynamic multi-task gradient balancing algorithms (such as GradNorm or PCGrad) to mitigate gradient conflict; the model ensemble relies on static heuristic aggregation rules rather than learned meta-classifiers; and the architecture lacks integration with geographical knowledge graphs or gazetteers to resolve localized place name ambiguities.
Future Work: Incorporating linked external content, including web pages and images posted alongside disaster tweets, into multimodal representation learning.; Extending the multi-task learning framework to support additional crisis informatics tasks across multiple diverse corpora.; Evaluating computational efficiency, inference latency, and high-throughput deployment architectures for real-time crisis message handling.; Integrating external knowledge maps, gazetteers, and geographical ontologies to disambiguate localized location references and enrich spatial context awareness.

Title: TweetTaglish: A Dataset for Investigating Tagalog-English Code-Switching
Authors: Megan Herrera; Ankit Aich; Natalie Parde
Venue: Proceedings of the Thirteenth Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (LREC 2022)
Domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Tagalog-English Code-Switching (Taglish), Social Media (Twitter), Low-Resource Languages
Problem Statement: Tagalog and Tagalog-English code-switching (Taglish) are under-represented in natural language processing research and practice, lacking large-scale annotated datasets, linguistic analysis, and standardized benchmarks for computational modeling and language distribution identification.
Theoretical Framework: Sociolinguistic theories of code-switching, including Goulet's (1968) six CS motivations, Bautista's (2004) framework on communicative efficiency and proficiency/deficiency drivers, Hamers and Blanc's (2000) and Poplack's (1980) three-way CS typology (inter-sentential, extra-sentential, intra-sentential), and Flores's (2020) empirical identification of Tagalog-English linguistic markers (bound morphemes, enclitics).
Methodology: Multilingual keyword harvesting on Twitter using six Tagalog CS-indicative linguistic features (magko-, di ba, talaga, ano yung, para sa, parang) across English and Filipino query settings to gather 21,150 tweets; preprocessing involving case normalization, stopword removal, and stripping of usernames, hashtags, emojis, punctuation, non-Roman text, and URLs; dictionary-based token-level language identification using PyEnchant for English, a scraped Tagalog lexicon, and rule-based morphological parsing for Tagalog verb conjugations; multi-label tweet-level language proportion assignment (percentages of English, Tagalog, and Other tokens); dataset validation via proof-of-concept regression modeling using 50-dimensional Filipino Word2Vec embeddings and six regressors (Mean baseline, OLS Linear, SVR, SGD, Bayesian Ridge, MLP) under an 80/20 train/test split.
Datasets and Benchmarks: TweetTaglish: 21,150 Tagalog-English code-switched and unilingual tweets collected from Twitter with word-level and tweet-level English, Tagalog, and Other language distribution annotations; Pretrained 50-dimensional Filipino Word2Vec embeddings trained on Philippine social media data (Marges, 2019)
Evaluation and Metrics: metrics: [R² (Coefficient of Determination); RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error); Cohen's Kappa (Inter-Annotator Agreement)]; inter annotator agreement: (instance level: κ = 0.70 (substantial agreement on 20 sample tweets), word level: κ = 0.15 (slight agreement due to Spanish cognates and morphological blending)); benchmark results: (MLP (Best): {'English': {'R2': 0.909, 'RMSE': 0.057}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.883, 'RMSE': 0.068}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.797, 'RMSE': 0.068}}, SVR: {'English': {'R2': 0.898, 'RMSE': 0.061}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.854, 'RMSE': 0.076}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.699, 'RMSE': 0.083}}, Linear: {'English': {'R2': 0.861, 'RMSE': 0.071}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.7, 'RMSE': 0.109}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.375, 'RMSE': 0.119}}, Ridge: {'English': {'R2': 0.861, 'RMSE': 0.071}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.7, 'RMSE': 0.109}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.374, 'RMSE': 0.119}}, SGD: {'English': {'R2': 0.848, 'RMSE': 0.074}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': 0.688, 'RMSE': 0.112}, 'Other': {'R2': 0.333, 'RMSE': 0.123}}, Mean Baseline: {'English': {'R2': -0.0, 'RMSE': 0.19}, 'Tagalog': {'R2': -6.32, 'RMSE': 0.2}, 'Other': {'R2': -0.0, 'RMSE': 0.151}})
Key Findings: Constructed TweetTaglish, a novel dataset containing 21,150 Tagalog-English code-switched and unilingual tweets with token-level and tweet-level language distribution annotations.; Validated dataset learnability through regression benchmarking, where all models substantially outperformed the Mean baseline, and the MLP regressor achieved the highest performance (English: R² = 0.909, RMSE = 0.057; Tagalog: R² = 0.883, RMSE = 0.068; Other: R² = 0.797, RMSE = 0.068).; Observed that regression models predicted English language distributions most accurately, while encountering the greatest difficulty predicting the 'Other' category.; Determined the overall corpus language distribution per tweet to average 55.2% Tagalog, 19.4% English, and 24.5% Other.; N-gram frequency analysis computationally validated the efficacy of Flores (2020) Tagalog linguistic features for harvesting Taglish text at scale, revealing high frequencies of personal pronouns ('ko', 'ako') characteristic of informal social media discourse.; Validation of dictionary-based annotation against a human speaker yielded substantial agreement at the instance level (κ = 0.70), though word-level agreement was lower (κ = 0.15) due to cross-lingual cognates and affixation.
Scope and Delimitations: Restricted to Tagalog-English code-switched text gathered from Twitter without geographic or user-specific constraints.; Data collection relies on six specific linguistic query terms (magko-, di ba, talaga, ano yung, para sa, parang) rather than comprehensive lexicon search.; Empirical evaluation is delimited to tweet-level language proportion regression rather than token-level sequence labeling, dependency parsing, or code-switching point detection.; Feature representation is limited to static 50-dimensional Word2Vec embeddings rather than contextualized multilingual transformer architectures.
Limitations (Summary): The keyword search strategy and dictionary-based language identification introduced noise from cross-lingual cognates (particularly Spanish words like 'para' misidentified as Tagalog), contributing to low word-level inter-annotator agreement (κ = 0.15). Additionally, regression models exhibited lower accuracy on the 'Other' category containing slang, misspellings, and hybrid morphological combinations.
Limitations (Verbatim Excerpt): One minor observation was that our current keyword search strategy allowed for the inclusion of text from some other non-English languages with similar phrases (e.g., Spanish, due to cognates such as para). This could be addressed in future iterations of data collection using more advanced regular expressions and text preprocessing techniques.
Generalizability Gap: The dataset is limited to Twitter and Tagalog-English code-switching, leaving unaddressed other Philippine regional languages (e.g., Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon), formal or spoken discourse modalities, other social media platforms, and non-Tagalog code-switching pairs.
Methodological Gap: Dictionary lookup paired with simple rule-based morphological parsing fails to robustly handle intra-word code-switching (Tagalog bound morphemes on English stems such as 'nakakatouch') and cross-lingual homographs/cognates; evaluations rely on static token-averaged 50-dimensional Word2Vec embeddings without comparing against contextualized multilingual language models.
Future Work: Experiment with more advanced NLP approaches to effectively process code-switching in everyday text and learn better representations for low-resource languages, including Taglish.; Employ advanced regular expressions and text preprocessing techniques to filter out non-target language text and cross-lingual cognates during data collection.; Explore more complex downstream code-switching tasks, such as word-level language identification, syntactic/dependency parsing, and code-switching point detection.
